Subject: 00 General
Comment: 14. Cycle 2 review comment [Repeated Comment] How is the torsional moment accounted for using this method. Note that torsional shear forces in individual pier may have different -/+ sign and cancel out when looking at the forces globally. Calculation pgs. 304 shows base shear = 1181.172k and pgs. 422 shows sum of pier reaction to equal around the same force, which does not make sense. Per structural calculation pgs. 326/597; CL28 there is 50,749.1 kip-ft of torsion on level 3, how is torsional force accounted for?  For example, this torsional moment distributed over a 41ft moment arm would equate to around 1200kips of shear on the Core piers. Wall CD on story3 shows only 53kips. Previous Comment  LATERAL DESIGN: Ref Struct Calcs. According to calc page 302, a majority of the shear forces at Level 3 are going into the longer walls to the west, Piers "CA" and "CB". Piers "CC" and "CD" resist only about 15 percent of the total forces. The total forces in these north-south walls total 1188 kips, which is very similar to the maximum "CORE" force of 1188.892 kips per Page  290. Because of the extreme torsional irregularity, it would be expected that the summation of wall forces from the individual walls be more than the "CORE" force. This is due to inherent torsionand accidental torsion multiplied by Ax. It would also be expected that the forces in pier "CD" would generally be a higher percentage of the overall wall forces due to its ability to resistance torsion. Because of these items, it's not clear if torsion is being properly considered in the analysis model. Please review the analysis model and confirm that inherent and accidental torsion is appropriately considered. Provide an ETABS output  Response  In the model all of the wall piers that comprise the stair and elevator core were labeled as “core” to take into account how those walls would act together during a seismic event.  Labeling the wall piers this way also allows you to take advantage of the effective flange widths/section of the adjacent wall piers per ACI 318-14 Section 18.10.5.2.  The section properties for each wall pier and their effective flange width within the core were then calculation so as to determine the relative stiffness of each pier.  Refer to calculations on CL15-CL21.  The loads from the core were then distributed to the individual piers based on their relative stiffness in comparison to the  other wall piers acting in the direction of the load.   As such the summation of CA, CB, CC, CD should equal the CORE force in the Y direction.  Refer to our response to 11A for how the inherent and accidental torsion is applied in the model.  Refer to CL129-CL163 for ETABS output. Structural Engineer (7)

Revise plans as needed. CYCLE #2: Cycle #2 Structural Calculations do not appear to include shear wall calculations per ACI 318-14 Section 18.10.4. Provide complete response with calculations, and revise plans as required. See below for details. ACI 318-14 Section 18.10.4.3 states:  "Walls shall have distributed shear reinforcement in two orthogonal directions in the plane of the wall. If hw/lw does not exceed 2.0, reinforcement ratio ρl shall be at least the reinforcement ratio ρt." hw = height of entire wall from base to top, or clear height of wall segment or wall pier considered, in. (base = seismic base) Assume seismic base is at 83'-2" (Level 1 - East) hw = 10'-2"+9'-6" = 19'-8" lw = length of entire wall, or length of wall segment or wall pier considered in direction of shear force, in. lw = 19.75' for east stair shear wall and west stair shear wall (3/S-311 and 11/S-311) hw/lw = 1.0 < 2.0, therefore, 18.10.4.3 applies and ρl (vertical distributed reinforcement ratio) shall be at least the reinforcement ratio ρt (horizontal distributed reinforcement ratio). This does not appear to be satisfied in Cycle #1 drawings (Cycle #2 plan set is missing some sheets such as S-301, and S-311). For example, the west stair shear wall appears to have horizontal reinforcing of #7@8" OC EF per 11/S-301, but vertical reinforcing of only #5@18" OC EF per 7/S-311.

Comment: 15. DEAD LOAD DUE TO LANDSCAPING CYCLE #1: SBC 1606.2 Design Dead Load      A. Landscape drawings show several high planters on elevated slabs, including 45" high bioretention planter on Level 2 (sheet L-112) and 42" high planters on Level 7 and Roof (sheets L-113 and L-114). Revise load maps and structural design to consider the maximum anticipated weight of the planters and their contents (i.e. planter self-weight, saturated soil, plantings at full maturity). If the intent is to use lightweight soil, coordinate with Landscape Architect to indicate maximum saturated soil density on Landscape plans.      B. Similarly, coordinate weight of saturated weight of green roof system with Landscape Architect, and indicate maximum saturated weight on Landscape plans. Revise structural design of roof to account for total weight of saturated green roof and roof assembly. CYCLE #2:       A. Load map sheets (S-011 through S-013) have not been provided. Level 2 slab design calculations provided (pages 96-120 of 280) do not show magnitudes of dead loads used for slab design, therefore, it is not possible to verify what dead loads were used for slab design, , such as whether weight of the 45" deep bioretention planter in the southeast corner was considered.  No response was provided for Levels 7 and Roof. As noted in Cycle #1, sheet L-115 shows Roof Level planters that are up to 42" deep and have significant areas (over 600sf). Assuming a saturated soil weight of 120 pcf would suggest a weight of 420 psf for a 42" deep planter excluding weight of the trees/plants, planter wall/base, roof finishes, and any items suspended from roof level slab. Dead load of 50psf is not adequate to account for the weight of planters shown on drawings. Provide detailed explanation that demonstrates that design is adequate or revise drawings to eliminate deep/heavy planters. See Cycle #1 comment for additional guidance and requirements.      B. CLOSED CYCLE #3:      A. It appears that the values in the Superimposed Dead Load Schedule for planters are based on a dead load of the floor of 15psf (including roofing and MEP allowance) and a soil density of 60pcf. For example: 30" soil depth *1ft/12" * 60pcf + 15psf = 165psf. There are several concerns here:           A1: soil density of 60pcf seems too low of a value to account for weight of saturated soil - ASCE 7-10 Chapter C3 provides values of up to 120pcf for earth: sand and gravel, wet. Weight density of water is 62.4psf, so assuming that saturated soil is 60psf would imply that it floats, which seems unrealistic.            A2: the soil depths assumed are lower than planter depths - only 30" of soil is assumed for 42" deep planters.            A3: the soil depth assumed for green roof appears to be 6", whereas section A1/L-502 indicates soil depth of +8".           A4: Most of the dead load of the roof is concentrated on the west half of the floor plate, therefore, assuming a uniform average dead load of 50psf throughout will underestimate seismic demands on the west side of the floor plate and overestimate seismic demands on the eastern half of the floor plate. This may result in overstress of some western shear walls and diaphragms. Revise plan set and design to consider a realistic and attainable saturated soil density and distribution. Structural Engineer consultant shall coordinate with Landscape Architect consultant and maximum saturated soil density (value in pcf) shall be indicated on landscape plans. If structural calculations assume a maximum soil depth that is lower than the overall planter depth, revise landscape plan at roof level (L-114) to indicate maximum soil depth, similar to level 7 (L-113). Note that this issue is nontrivial: using a higher soil density (such as 80psf) and soil depth equal to planter depths shown on landscape plans can increase total dead load on roof by 30%.      B. See item A3 above.      C. (NEW CORRECTION) It appears that the Level 07 Load Map specifies wood decking (A18) in two locations where planters with 18" of soil (A15) should be specified. Revise 1/S-013.

Calculations  that demonstrate that the elements supporting discontinuous walls are designed to resist seismic load effects including overstrength factor of Section 12.4.3 for the entire load path down to the foundation. This includes the connections of the elements along the load path. CYCLE #2:       A. CLOSED      B. Calculations provided do not appear to correctly implement the Overstrength Factor of Section 12.4.3. Per Table 12.2-1, it appears that Overstrength Factor is 3, which appears to be confirmed by W_0 value noted on page 35 of 280 of calculations. Calculations on pages 178 and 179 of 280 indicate "DEMANDS INCREASED PER ASCE 7-10 12.4.3.1" for discontinous walls, however, the shear demands (v, plf) appear to be only about 1.5 to 1.8 times greater than the average shear demands of the shear walls at that level, which is significantly less than Overstrength Factor of 3. Response to Cycle #2 stated:  "A capacity based design approach was used using expected yield strengths of the holdown rods per the AISC Sesimic Design Manual. The Ry was taken as 1.5 and represents the material overstrength used instead of the system overstrength per ASCE 7-16." It appears that the intent is to use ASCE 7-10 Section 12.4.3.1 Exception, which states: "The value of Emh need not exceed the maximum force that can develop in the element as determined by a rational, plastic mechanism analysis or nonlinear response analysis utilizing realistic expected values of material strengths." Provide calculations that demonstrate the value of "maximum force that can develop in the element". This value will be higher than Ry=1.5 because it does not use resistance factors (phi) and because actual hardware that is selected usually has a higher capacity than the demand (i.e. DCR < 1.0). Consequently, the ratio of maximum force that can develop in an element divided by its usable capacity will exceed 1.5. This correction will remain open until conformance with relevant codes and standards is demonstrated.

Subject: Tree requirements (SMC 23.44.008)
Comment: This project is subject to the tree standards in what was SMC 23.44.008.I which state: I.Tree Requirements. 1.Trees are required when single-family dwelling units are constructed. The minimum number of caliper inches of tree required per lot may be met by using either the tree preservation option or tree planting option described in subsections 23.44.008.I.1.a. or I.1.b., or by a combination of preservation and planting. This requirement may be met by planting or preserving street trees in the public right-of-way. Submerged land shall not be included in calculating lot area for purposes of either the tree preservation option or tree planting option. a.Tree Preservation Option. For lots over 3,000 square feet, at least 2 caliper inches of existing tree per 1,000 square feet of lot area must be preserved. On lots that are 3,000 square feet or smaller, at least 3 caliper inches of existing tree must be preserved per lot. When this option is used, a tree preservation plan is required. b.Tree Planting Option. For lots over 3,000 square feet, at least 2 caliper inches of tree per 1,000 square feet of lot area must be planted. On lots that are 3,000 square feet or smaller, at least 3 caliper inches of tree must be planted per lot. 2.Tree Measurements. Trees planted to meet the requirements in subsection 23.44.008.I.1 shall be at least 1.5 inches in diameter. The diameter of new trees shall be measured (in caliper inches) 6 inches above the ground. Existing trees shall be measured 4.5 feet above the ground. When an existing tree is 3 to 10 inches in diameter, each 1 inch counts as 1 inch toward meeting the tree requirements in subsection 23.44.008.I.1. When an existing tree is more than 10 inches in diameter, each 1 inch of the tree that is over 10 inches shall count as 3 inches toward meeting the tree requirement. 3.Tree Preservation Plans. If the tree preservation option is chosen, a tree preservation plan must be submitted and approved. Tree preservation plans shall provide for protection of trees during construction according to standards promulgated by the Director.

Subject: Temporary Shoring and Excavation plan
Comment: SMC 25.09.330 B.6. and SMC 22.170.070 B.2.c. Temporary Excavation and Shoring Sheet A1.2 includes notes that indicate that an ultra block shoring wall will be used, and that the Geotechnical Special Inspector shall continuously monitor installation of the ultra block wall. The subsurface soil conditions include very loose fill and topsoil, underlain by wet, loose silt with organics.  These soil types do not work well with ultra block shoring, which is likely why the use of ultra  block shoring was not included in the 2019 report by Geotech Consultants. The notes on the right side of Sheet A1.2 include a description of slot cuts for this project, a method that was not evaluated in the 2019 report by Geotech Consultants. Upload an addendum to the geotechnical engineering report with methods for excavation of the loose topsoil and fill soil for this project, and update the temporary excavation system accordingly. Make sure the temporary excavation and shoring system includes the existing grade contours, and that the excavation reaches the anticipated bearing depth, which is about 5 feet beneath the existing ground surface. The temporary excavation and shoring system needs to demonstrate that adjacent properties are protected during construction.Dean Griswold (4)

Comment: Drainage Review is required for this project per the 2021 Seattle Stormwater  Manual Volume 1, Chapter 8, since there is 750 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface and/or 5,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new and replaced hard surface associated with the project. Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas, driveways, walkways, and parking areas. Permeable pavement and pavers are considered a hard surface.      Please complete and submit the following documents: 1) Standard Construction Stormwater Control and Soil Amendment  (CSC/SOIL) Plan 2) Standard Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan 3) On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (full workbook) 4) Infiltration Evaluation Documentation / Infiltration Test Checklist The following are the Approved Points of Discharge for the project: a) The "Approved Point of Stormwater Discharge" is "Onsite". b) The "Drainage Basin" is "N/A for Single Family Projects". (Is this a SFR with Dadu or is this two stand alone SFR's?) If it is a SFR, Dadu combination it would be Single Family. Anything else is Parcel based. c) The "Approved Point of Wastewater Discharge" is "Sanitary" d) The "Approved Point of Subsurface Discharge" is "Onsite". The Seattle Stormwater Manual and all of the templates and documents mentioned above are available at http://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code. The CSC/SOIL Plan and DWC Plan must be combined with the submitted Plan Set PDF.Shomari Anderson (4)

Subject: Capacity Constrained - Peak Flow Control Standard
Comment: Since this development site discharges to a downstream system that is considered to be Capacity Constrained and the total new plus replaced hard surface is 2,000 square feet or more, the Peak Flow Control Standard is required per the Seattle Stormwater Manual Vol. 1, Section 4.4.3.5   Note: the Peak Flow Control Standard was changed in the 2021 Stormwater Code to a more stringent standard per Section 5.3.5.   Please demonstrate on the Preliminary DWC Plan how the Peak Flow Control Standard will be achieved and include the calculations in the Preliminary Drainage Report. Also Note: Projects with less than 10,000 square feet of new plus replaced hard surface may use the Pre-Sized Flow Control Calculator in lieu of performing a hydrologic analysis using a continuous rainfall-runoff model. Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: Revegetation requirements apply within ECAs even if an exemption or other ECA relief is granted. The standards of SMC 25.09.070 apply when any of the following activities occur within ECAs and their buffers: planting, disturbing, or removing trees and/or vegetation; adding, altering, or removing impervious surface; or other land disturbing activity. Please provide the following so we can determine the extent of tree and vegetation removal necessary and whether any impacts to ECA ecological functions are adequately mitigated in the plan set. A. New L mitigation sheet: Provide EXISTING ground coverage conditions on landscape mitigation site plan and table. ECA code section SMC 25.09.065 requires that you avoid or minimize tree and vegetation removal within ECAs. Since relief has been granted, you do not need to show a buffer, only steep slope hazard area on the mapped lot. - Provide a brief description of the EXISTING ground coverage within these areas. Examples of ground coverage include: lawn, ornamental landscaping, blackberry or other invasive species, trees, patio, pathway. - Show locations of all existing trees (use table on A1.0) within the ECA to be removed and/or retained. - Clearly delineate the "Steep Slopes (ECA1)" on the landscape mitigation sheet. The SDCI External GIS Map is a helpful tool to locate designated ECAs. https://seattlecitygis.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=f822b2c6498c4163b0 cf908e2241e9c2 B. New L mitigation sheet: Mitigation is required for lost ecological function when trees and vegetation are removed within the ECAs. Include a brief summary of the existing ecological functions performed by the ECA on and adjacent to the site. The ecological functions include but may not be limited to: habitat for amphibian, avian, and terrestrial wildlife species; soil stabilization; and stormwater filtering, detention, and infiltration. C. New L mitigation sheet: Provide a PROPOSED landscape mitigation plan and table showing the location, size, species, quantities and spacing of trees/shrubs newly planted as a result of ECA areas impacted for site development. Use L1 plant schedule proposed native plantings only. https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Forms/TreeVegetationStandardMitigatio nPlan.pdf - New trees must be two gallon size and shrubs one gallon on the planting schedule.  - No permanent irrigation is allowed in mapped ECA steep slope erosion hazard areas. - Planting selections shall be native species suited to specific site conditions/orientation, no cultivars. Add a note that areas that have been cleared, graded, or compacted are to be amended with organic matter prior to planting.Revegetation (2)

Subject: Listed Creek Flow Control Pre-developed Pasture
Comment: Since this project discharges to a Listed Creek Basin and the total new plus replaced hard surface is 5,000 square feet or more, it is required to provide flow control meeting the Pre-developed Pasture Standard per Seattle Stormwater Manual Volume 1, Sections 4.4.3.2 and 5.3.3.  Please demonstrate how this flow control standard will be met on the plans and in the Drainage Report.  Note: Projects with less than 10,000 square feet of new plus replaced hard surface may use the Pre-Sized Flow Control Calculator in lieu of performing a hydrologic analysis using a continuous rainfall-runoff model.  The Pre-Sized Flow Control Calculator is available on the Stormwater Code webpage at http://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code.

Subject: OSM Calculator Required - Parcel-Based
Comment: Per SMC 22.805.050.B, Parcel Based Projects with more than 1,500 square feet of New Plus Replaced Hard Surfaces or 7,000 square feet of Land Disturbing Activities (or 750 square feet of New Plus Replaced Hard Surface if the project is on a lot that was either created or altered in size on or after January 1, 2016) must meet the requirements for On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) per SMC 22.805.070.   Please provide OSM BMPs as required (see the Seattle 2021 Stormwater Manual Vol. 1, Sections 4.4.5 and 5.2 and Vol. 3, Chapter 3) and complete the On-site Stormwater Management – List Approach Calculator.  A link to a live spreadsheet of the On-Site Stormwater Management – List Approach Calculator can be found at the following website under the Required Forms in the 2016 Stormwater Code and Manual Section: http://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code  Please use the spreadsheet at the link to document OSM BMP selection, BMP sizing, and infeasibility of any BMP ’s that are not selected.  Please include a PDF copy of the whole workbook along with the next submittal.

Subject: Special Inspector nomination

The Inspection Agency must be the same engineer/firm that prepared the geotechnical report. If the owner nominates a different engineer/firm to act as the Geotechnical Special Inspector, the new engineer must review the original geotechnical report and submit a letter indicating a review was performed, along with a statement of agreement with the evaluation and provisions contained in the report. If the new engineer does not agree with aspects of the report, rebuttal evaluations and recommendations must be included in the review letter. The plans must be revised accordingly and submitted to SDCI for review. Please do not fill in special inspection items on the enclosed form. Subject: 11 Accessibility
Comment: 22.Refer. to live/work units shown on sheet A-111, it shows that there are steps from street 20th Ave NW to live/work units 113 and 114. Per SBC 1104.5, accessible route shall be coincide with or be located in the same area as a general circulation path. Route from lobby through corridor to units 113 and 114 is not general circulation path. Also, per SBC 1104.5, accessible route shall not pass through kitchen. Please revise the design, so live/work 113 and 114 will meet accessible route requirement. Cycle 1 Response: Level 1 has been redesigned and has only on Live/Work Unit. The north entry is an accessible route and is part of the general path of circulation. Per SBC 1104.5, Exception 2, “a single accessible route is permitted to pass through a kitchen … in an Accessible Unit, Type A Unit. ” The Live/Work unit on Level one is a Type A Unit. Correction Cycle #2: Though level 1 has been redesigned and there is an accessible path through ramp and door 109B to live/work unit, the general path of circulation to live/work unit is still through exterior door 108.  Also note that Exception 2 in SBC Section 1104.5 means for its residential portion.  Work portion in live/work unit is nonresidential and exception 2 doesn't apply.   Please label the interior entrance door from corridor to live/work unit 108 and make sure that door meets corridor fire rating requirement per SBC Table 1020.1 Due to redesign, three-step is added from lobby to interior space.  The route from exterior through ramp/stair case is not a general circulation path.  Please provide accessible path on general path of circulation for live/work unit and lobby.

Comment: 4.Refer. to sheet A-115 roof plan and occupant load calculation on sheet G-008, it shows roof level has more than 50 occupant load. Also, in order to be considered a portion of floor below, a penthouse shall be used only to shelter mechanical equipment, exit stairway or vertical shaft openings. Please either: 1)Revise the plans to reduce the area of the penthouse; or 2)Show that the area provided is necessary to accommodate the equipment, shafts and stairs. Note that only 5-story is allowed for R2 occupancy for type IIIA building. Cycle 1 Response: Please refer to Sheet G-009 Drawing A5 showing a total occupancy of 42 at roof level. The area calculated assumes that egress path is not part of the total occupiable area calculation. Correction Cycle #2: Though occupant load calculation was modified on sheet G-009 to show total occupant load is less than 50, the area shown on Roof Level A1 on sheet A-115 is more than the ones used in calculations. For example, outdoor amenity west is 404 sf, only 239 sf was used in calculation; outdoor amenity east is 377 sf, only 222 sf was used; area between grids 4.3/5 and grids B/C.2 needs to be included.  Note that path area is allowed to be excluded only when its width is not greater than 3' and when the path is connecting two areas.  SDCI doesn't allow exclude a path which is part of one assembly area.  Please reduce the assembly area on the roof deck if SBC Interpretation I509.2 is intended to be used. 54'-1

ACI 318-14 section 9.7.2.2 - spacing of bonded longitudinal reinforcement closest to the tension face appears to exceed s given in section 24.3.      B. Subject: 18 Foundations & Retaining Walls
Comment: 5. FOUNDATIONS AT SHEAR WALLS At some locations, holdowns appear to have significant tension demands, compared to the counteracting dead load. Director's Rule 10-2009 allows the use of pin piles for axial compressive loading only (no tension). Some examples are noted below. Provide calculations that demonstrate that the structure shown in plans has adequate dead load to counteract uplift forces due to seismic and wind lateral loads without subjecting pin piles to tensile loading. Use load combinations per SBC 1605 or ASCE 7-16. Revise plans as appropriate.      A. Example 1: HDU8 holdown shown on sheet S2.1 at the north end of the SW6 shear wall on the east side of the AADU bedroom is noted in calculations (page 6 of 67) to have a seismic holdown demand of 8226 lbs. This holdown is anchored to a small foundation shown in section 10/S3.1. Framing span is north-south for most levels, so tributary load to this wall from stories above appears to be very low.       B. Example 2: HDU8 holdowns shown on sheet S2.1 along wall that separates AADU from stair and utility room appears to be anchored to a small foundation shown in section 10/S3.1 that appears to have inadequate flexural and/or shear capacity to distribute concentrated loads (due to shear wall overturning) to engage sufficient counteracting dead load.

Subject: 19 Concrete
Comment: 6. SLAB-ON-GRADE Several details (such as 7/S3.1, 12/S3.1, 1/S4.3) appear to indicate reinforcing bars between critical concrete elements (cantilever slabs, foundations, cantilever beams) and the slab-on-grade. Slab joints, construction joints, and thermal breaks typically provided at non-structural slab on grade would compromise the integrity of this reinforcing and may lead to structural failure. If the intent is to provide structural slab on grade, revise plan set to indicate such, and revise sections and details accordingly. Coordinate with architect the consequences of thermal breaks on structural and energy code requirements.

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: 7. ELEMENTS SUPPORTING DISCONTINUOUS WALLS OR FRAMES ASCE 7-16 Section 12.3.3.3 - Structural elements supporting discontinuous shear walls shall be designed to resist the seismic load effects including overstrength factor. Overstrength factor shall be applied to seismic load effects for all elements and connections in the load path, from location of discontinuity to the foundation (i.e. beams, connections, columns, etc.)  Verify all locations where elements support discontinous walls or frames. Revise plans and calculations to demonstrate that all elements and their connections in the load path to the foundation are adequate to resist all loads and consider all directions of loading.  Example: Calculation for Main Floor beam labeled Cont PSL 5 1/4 x 14 appears to be provided on page 43 of 67 of structural calculations. The cantilever portion of this beam supports discontinous shear wall SW6 above, which appears to result in a maximum reaction of 21,203 lbs at support 2. Plans show 6x6 post at column 2, which appears inadequate to resist a reaction of 21,203 lbs. There are several other locations where loads are discontinuous and appear to require strengthening to provide adequate load path to foundations. Revise calculations and plans and demonstrate compliance at all discontinuous shear walls.

Revise to consider all loads from the structure above, including critical locations such as posts, holdowns at ends of shear walls, etc. Similar issues appear to occur at section 8/S3.1 and structural calculations pages 64-67. Subject: 0 New Plan Review Process
Comment: On January 10, SDCI transitioned to providing plan reviews via plan mark-up instead of traditional letters. We appreciate your understanding as we rolled out the technology and staff learned new procedures. The primary change that we are asking of applicants is that they document responses to comments directly in the plan set provided to them by SDCI at the end of each review cycle instead of sending letters corresponding to each correction letter. When all responses are documented, we ask that applicants upload the response plan set (as document type Correction Response Plan Set or Correction Response Plan Set – Land Use) along with the new, clean plan set as (document type Plan Set or Plan Set – Land Use) for the next review cycle. We have a video to help you learn how to navigate the new process here:  https://youtu.be/KB8laufkd7M. As we transition to delivering marked up plan sets, you may receive both letters and marked up plan sets with our corrections documented. As a rule, please respond to any letter you receive with a letter and any marked-up plan set by embedding your responses in the marked-up plan set. We recognize that this transition requires changes to how you respond to our correction reports. We firmly believe that the changes we are instituting will lead to a reduction in the number of review cycles required to issue a permit. Remember, you will still: %ª Receive email notifications that a review has been completed. %ª Find review summary reports by discipline in the Seattle Services Portal as they are completed. %ª Submit updated plan sets after all reviews have been completed. What will be new is: %ª When all reviews are completed, you will receive a marked-up plan set which contains the comments from ALL the review disciplines. %ª Instead of preparing responses to each individual correction letter as you do today, you will be asked to reply to the comments directly in the marked-up plan set using either Bluebeam (requires a license) or Adobe Acrobat (free). Comment: FOR INFORMATION ONLY. NO RESPONSE REQUIRED. On January 10, SDCI transitioned to providing plan reviews via plan mark-up instead of traditional letters. We appreciate your understanding as we rolled out the technology and staff learned new procedures. The primary change that we are asking of applicants is that they document responses to comments directly in the plan set provided to them by SDCI at the end of each review cycle instead of sending letters corresponding to each correction letter. When all responses are documented, we ask that applicants upload the response plan set (as document type Correction Response Plan Set or Correction Response Plan Set – Land Use) along with the new, clean plan set as (document type Plan Set or Plan Set – Land Use) for the next review cycle. We have a video to help you learn how to navigate the new process here:  https://youtu.be/KB8laufkd7M. As we transition to delivering marked up plan sets, you may receive both letters and marked up plan sets with our corrections documented. As a rule, please respond to any letter you receive with a letter and any marked-up plan set by embedding your responses in the marked-up plan set. We recognize that this transition requires changes to how you respond to our correction reports. We firmly believe that the changes we are instituting will lead to a reduction in the number of review cycles required to issue a permit. Remember, you will still: %ª Receive email notifications that a review has been completed. %ª Find review summary reports by discipline in the Seattle Services Portal as they are completed. %ª Submit updated plan sets after all reviews have been completed. What will be new is: %ª When all reviews are completed, you will receive a marked-up plan set which contains the comments from ALL the review disciplines. %ª Instead of preparing responses to each individual correction letter as you do today, you will be asked to reply to the comments directly in the marked-up plan set using either Bluebeam (requires a license) or Adobe Acrobat (free). If you work with subconsultants, you will need to coordinate with them to include their comments in your response plan set. Lastly, please help us perform reviews more efficiently! As we have worked on this transition, many of our reviewers indicated that they rely on bookmarks to navigate the (sometimes lengthy) plan sets that we receive from applicants. One thing that would allow us to review more quickly is to have applicants include a good set of bookmarks in every plan set that is submitted. Please follow the requirements for submitting pdf documents, outlined in Tip 106, General Standards for Plans and Drawings, to include a good set of bookmarks in every plan set you submit

Subject: 00 General
Comment: Revised Code of Washington (RCW) 64.55.005 requires that the developers of multi-unit residential buildings comply with one of the three options listed below. Indicate which option will be used and provide electronic copies of the required documents as specified. (1) a. Submit plans, details, and specifications for the  construction of the building enclosure, per RCW 64.55.010(2). The building enclosure design documents must be signed and sealed by an architect or engineer licensed in the State of Washington, per RCW 64.55.10(3). b. Provide a statement on the plans or in a letter, signed and stamped as above, in substantially the following form: "The undersigned has provided building enclosure documents that in my professional judgment are appropriate to satisfy the requirements of RCW 64.55.005 through 64.55.090." c. Submit to the building inspector, a letter signed by a third-party qualified inspector certifying that the building enclosure has been inspected during construction and has been constructed in substantial compliance with the building enclosure design documents, per RCW 64.55.060. A final inspection will not be approved, nor a final certificate of occupancy issued prior to the receipt of the signed letter. (2) Submit a completed, signed, and recorded Condominium Sales Prohibition Covenant which prohibits the sale of individual dwelling units as condominiums for a minimum of five years. The completed and signed form must be recorded with the King County Recorder's office and submitted prior to permit issuance, per RCW 64.55.020(10). (3) Demonstrate RCW 64.55 does not apply by submitting an approved and recorded unit lot subdivision, prior to issuance of the construction permit. DENOTES   DOOR

Subject: Special Inspector nomination
Comment: SMC 22.170.130. Nominate a geotechnical engineering firm on the enclosed SDCI Geotechnical Special Inspections Schedule form. This form must be signed by the owner or owner's representative; the form cannot be signed by the contractor nor the geotechnical engineer.      The Inspection Agency must be the same engineer/firm that prepared the geotechnical report. If the owner nominates a different engineer/firm to act as the Geotechnical Special Inspector, the new engineer must review the original geotechnical report and submit a letter indicating a review was performed, along with a statement of agreement with the evaluation and provisions contained in the report. If the new engineer does not agree with aspects of the report, rebuttal evaluations and recommendations must be included in the review letter. The plans must be revised accordingly and submitted to SDCI for review. Please do not fill in special inspection items on the enclosed form.     Requests for changes of Special Inspection Agency that occur during plan review should be submitted with corrected plans. If the request occurs after permit issuance, send the materials to jerry.abson@seattle.gov.

Subject: General
Comment: [DWC PLAN] Please provide the slope information on the permeable pavement surfaces (PPS). The walkways sloping south from the middle of the project site, appears to have a slope greater than 2.0%.  If the subgrade slope is greater than 2.0%, the following criteria must be considered while modeling the PPS surfaces using WWHM. 1.When the subgrade slopes is greater than 2% and the permeable pavement surfaces do not contain internal check dams, then use a total effective depth of 1-inch in the stormwater modelling. 2.When the subgrade slopes is greater than 2% and internal check dams are proposed within the permeable pavement surfaces, each cell of the permeable pavement that is separated by internal check dams shall be modelled separately. The dimensions of each stipulated cell shall be equal to the below grade base materials with a storage depth equal to the average depth of water behind the downstream check dam. Please provide additional information in the form of a site – specific detail (cross – section) of the permeable pavement showing the average depth and check dam dimensions, when using this approach.

The proposed infiltration facility appears to be 5.5 feet deep from the surrounding grades. Alternatively, the infiltration facility maybe redesigned with a shallower depth.

Comment: SMC 23.45.536 (Parking Location, Access, and Screening):  It appears the two existing parking spaces/gravel driveways are not meeting what was permitted for 6206427-CN in 2009 when the garage was removed. As the development is in a Frequent Transit Service Area (FTSA) and in the Rainer Beach Urban Village, parking is not required. Therefore, the development must meet what was permitted in 2009 or the parking must be removed. If the parking is removed, the curb and curb cut must be replaced per SDOT standards. Alternatively, if you do not want to meet what was permitted in 2009 and you do not want to remove parking, you can propose parking that meets current development standards. Current parking and access development standards include providing an 8' x 16' parking space with electric vehicle charging infrastructure. Additionally, as 51st Ave S. is an Minor Arterial and the proposed use is either an apartment or a rowhouse, a vehicle cannot back onto 51st Ave S. from the parking area per SMC 23.54.030.D.1.f.1. Therefore, there must be a way for the car to turn around on-site before exiting onto 51st Ave S. If you have additional questions about parking and access, please send me an email to discuss further prior to the next round of corrections.

Subject: Zoning – SMC 23.45 – Multifamily
Comment: SMC 23.45.518 (Setbacks and Separations): Side Setback: The required side setback for an apartment is 5' and the side setback for a rowhouse is 3.5' per Table A for SMC 23.45.518. It appears that the existing side setback on the east side of the development is nonconforming to current development standards. Please provide additional documents that show the use of the structure when it was originally permitted. If the structure was originally permitted as a single-family house, the existing nonconformity may remain per SMC 23.45.518.J.2. By adding the additional unit and changing the use from a duplex to an apartment building, the existing nonconformity (i.e. the 3' setback) increases from .5' (i.e. the required rowhouse setback) to 2' (i.e. the required apartment setback). If the structure was permitted as a duplex, SMC 23.45.518.J does not apply and SMC 23.42.112.B would apply and with that said, if the proposed unit becomes an AADU instead of a new unit, the existing nonconformity is allowed to remain as it will not increase or expand the existing nonconformity. If you have any additional questions about this correction, please email me to discuss further prior to the next round of corrections.

Comment: SMC 23.58B/23.58C (Mandatory Housing Affordability): MHA General Compliance: In accordance with SMC 23.45.51, your project is subject to the Mandatory Housing Affordability (MHA) under SMC Chapter 23.58C for residential development. Please provide documentation in the plan set showing how the project will address the affordable housing requirements using either the payment or performance options. This includes, but is not limited to, summary tables showing the calculation of payment or performance amounts (as indicated on page 3 in Tip Sheet 257), submittal of a draft housing agreement, if required, and documentation on the floor plans of any performance MHA units, if required. Please see Tip Sheet 257 for more information for how to display the MHA calculations and requirements in the plans. If the payment option is chosen, please note that this project is located in an M Low area and vested on 2/23/2022. This date affects the fee applicable, as shown in Tip Sheet 257. If the performance option is elected, a housing agreement is required prior to the issuance of this permit. Please contact Prithy Korathu (prithy.korathu@seattle.gov) to initiate the review process of the housing agreement and complete the Office of Housing review and approvals. Please group all floor area diagrams, FAR, and MHA information together in the plans, in sequential sheets at or near the beginning of the plan set. This is required to ensure accuracy, facilitate reviews, and provide better transparency in permit plan records. The floor area diagrams should include all gross floor area in the project and indicate whether floor area is chargeable for the FAR calculation. If needed for the MHA calculation, the use should also be indicated on the floor area diagrams (e.g., commercial, residential, live-work, or other non-residential use). Alternatively, if the proposed unit is changed to be a Attached Accessory Dwelling Unit (AADU) accessory to Unit 1, MHA does not apply as an AADU is not considered a unit per the definition of "unit" in SMC 23.58C.020. If you elect to go the AADU path instead of the new unit path, you will need to update the project description and ensure all relevant requirements in SMC 23.45 are met for the addition of an AADU. Subject: Zoning – SMC 23.58B and 23.58C – Mandatory
Comment: SMC 23.58B/23.58C (Mandatory Housing Affordability): MHA-R - Gross Floor Area - Payment Option: All residential gross floor area is countable for MHA-R, except as expressly provided under SMC 23.58C.040.A. It is still unclear how the gross floor area of the structure was calculated. Per SMC 23.84A.014, gross floor area is the number of square feet of total floor area bounded by the inside surface of the exterior wall of the structure as measured at the floor line, and any additional areas identified as gross floor area within a zone. Additionally, per Director's Rule 4-2019, floors or partial floors that have a floor to ceiling height of at least 7' are counted as gross floor area. In order to clarify the gross floor area of each floor, please provide a diagram of each floor that includes the dimensions of each floor measured from the interior of the exterior wall. This includes the bay windows on the main floor and the area under the dormer on the upper floor. This may also include the attic space, or portions of the attic space, if the floor to ceiling height is 7 or more feet. Although the floor area is not changing with this proposal, an accurate gross floor area is required to determine the accurate MHA costs. If you have additional questions about this correction, please call me at (206) 531-5822.MHA (3)

An extension of the public storm drain is required across the full frontage of the property per SMC 22.805.020.L and the SPU Public Drainage System Director's Rule DWW-210. SMC 22.800.080.I: Unless an adjustment per subsection SMC 22.800.040.B or an exception per subsection SMC 22.800.040.C is approved by the Director, an owner or occupant who is required, or who wishes, to connect to a public drainage system shall be required to extend the public drainage system if a public drainage system is not accessible within an abutting public area across the full frontage of the property. This main extension may be eligible to enter into a Latecomer Agreement. Latecomer agreements allow a property owner who has installed drainage utility system improvements to recover a portion of the costs of those improvements from other property owners who later connect to the improvements. For more information, please visit the website or contact the SPU Development Services Office at spu_dso@seattle.gov or (206) 684-3333. Subject: PE Evaluation & Certification Required
Comment: If you intend to reuse existing side sewer, an Evaluation and Certification of the existing side sewers by a Professional Engineer is necessary because the existing side sewer/s were installed prior to 2004.   SS Code 21.16.240 and the Requirements for Design and Construction of Side Sewers Director's Rule (DR 4-2011) detail the requirements for use of an existing side sewer. In summary, a civil engineer must evaluate and certify the existing side sewer; if the side sewer is 50 years or older, the side sewer will need to be lined; if the existing side sewer is less than 50 years old, the side sewer must either be lined or the Evaluation and Certification process must include a pressure test. Please add  a very clear, boxed note added to the Drainage and Wastewater Control Plan that  the existing side sewer must be Evaluated and Certified by a Professional Engineer and either rehabilitated (i.e. lined) or pressure tested all the way to the public mainline in the street.  The completed Evaluation and Certification form must be submitted to the inspector during construction.  The form is available with the following link: http://www.seattle.gov/dpd/permits/permittypes/sidesewer/default.htm

Per the Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 5.4.4.5 …Bioretention Cells that receive runoff from more than 5,000 square feet must be divided into at least 2 cells and the runoff must be directed to an upstream cell in a bioretention series (interconnected series of cells). 2) Please show a series of interconnected bioretention cells for the bioretention facilities that receive runoff from more than 5,000 sf of impervious area and show where the inlet to the upstream cell is and where the outlet in the downstream cell is on the Drainage Plans. Individual cells are defined as separate ponding areas delineated by distinct overflow weir. 3) Please clarify if the roof areas L7, L6, L5 and L2 are contributory to this single facility. The stormwater plan (sheet C401) and the OSM plan (sheet C402) do not match, provide consistent information on all plan sheets. 4) Provide a site specific detail of this non-infiltrating bioretention facility in series and call out the inflow invert, overflow elevation, underdrain invert, pond bottom elevation, top of wall elevation, ponding depth and freeboard. Call out the weir wall elevation and note that the top of weir shall match the overflow elevation within the upstream cell. Also, note that the aggregate layer above the underdrain and below the bioretention soil shall be a minimum of 12-inch.

Subject: Seismic Site Class
Comment: ASCE 7-16, Chapter 20.  The uploaded geotechnical addendum assumed Site Class D for determining seismic coefficients. In order to categorize as Site Class D, please demonstrate either of the followings: a)  Shear wave velocity for the top 100 ft is 600 to 1,200 ft/s b)  SPT-N blow counts for the top 100 ft is 15 to 50 per feet. c)  Undrained shear strength for the top 100 ft is 1,000 to 2,000lb/ft2. OR, based on the boring logs provided in above-referenced geotechnical report, the Site Class should be categorized as Site Class C or default Site Class D.

Subject: Subgrade and bearing pressure

Subject: Special Inspector nomination
Comment: SMC 22.170.130. Nominate a geotechnical engineering firm on the SDCI Geotechnical Special Inspections Schedule form. The form  is named as " Special Inspection Notification" and can be found on the project portal. This form must be signed by the owner or owner's representative; the form cannot be signed by the contractor nor the geotechnical engineer.      The Inspection Agency must be the same engineer/firm that prepared the geotechnical report. If the owner nominates a different engineer/firm to act as the Geotechnical Special Inspector, the new engineer must review the original geotechnical report and submit a letter indicating a review was performed, along with a statement of agreement with the evaluation and provisions contained in the report. If the new engineer does not agree with aspects of the report, rebuttal evaluations and recommendations must be included in the review letter. The plans must be revised accordingly and submitted to SDCI for review. Please do not fill in special inspection items on the enclosed form.    Requests for changes of Special Inspection Agency that occur during plan review should be submitted with corrected plans. If the request occurs after permit issuance, send the materials to the geotechnical reviewer.

Subject: Drainage Review
Comment: The project is proposing to connect to the private side sewer that serves 308 35th Ave E and 311 36th Ave E.  I'm not finding any evidence that this site has the right to connect to that private side sewer.  The Preliminary Assessment Reports note the approved point of discharge as the public combined main in the unopened right of way of E Thomas St.  Because of this, a completed, signed, and notarized Side Sewer Joint Use and Maintenance Agreement (JUMA) is required for approval of the Drainage Review for this project. Submittal of this document cannot be deferred to the Side Sewer Permit for this situation. Recording of the document will not be required until the Side Sewer Permit Application but it is strongly recommended that the documents be completed and recorded under this Drainage Review. If there is an existing recorded Side Sewer Joint Use and Maintenance Agreement, please provide a copy. If a signed JUMA cannot be provided, the project will need to connect to the combined main in E Thomas St.4 (1)

Subject: Performance monitoring notes
Comment: SMC 22.170.110 A. Please modify the shoring monitoring notes on Sheet SH1.0 to reflect the following SDCI minimum monitoring requirements:  *Indicate on the plan the minimum monitoring point spacing along the top of the wall and minimum distance behind the wall that reflect the recommendations provided by the geotechnical engineer.  *Establish a baseline reading of monitoring points on the ground surface and settlement-sensitive structures behind the shoring wall alignment prior to dewatering, excavation, and installation of the shoring systems.  *A licensed surveyor (not the contractor) must do the surveying at least once a week.   *Survey frequency can be decreased after the shoring system has been installed and excavation is complete if the data indicates little or no additional movement. Surveying must continue until the permanent structure (including floor slabs as braces) is complete up to final and street grades. The survey frequency will be determined by the geotechnical engineer after review and approval by SDCI and SDOT.  *The geotechnical engineer shall review survey data and provide an evaluation of wall performance along with survey data to SDCI and SDOT on at least a weekly basis. Immediately and directly, notify SDCI and SDOT if any unusual or significantly increased movement occurs. *Immediately and directly notify the geotechnical and structural engineers, wall designer, SDCI, and SDOT if 0.5 inches of movement occurs between two consecutive readings and when total movements reach 0.5 inch. At that amount of movement, the engineers and designers shall determine the cause of displacement and develop remedial measures sufficient to limit total wall movements to 1 inch. All earthwork and construction activities must be directed towards immediate implementation of remedial measures necessary to limit total wall movements to what has been defined as acceptable by the design team SDCI and SDOT (as indicated above).

Subject: Lateral Analysis
Comment: 17. WOOD LATERAL: Ref Wood Framing Plans. The open-front diaphragm at the northeast and northwest portions of the building appear to exceed the maximum limit of  L'=35 feet per SDPWS 4.2.5.2. Review this condition and revise design as necessary or provide further justification for the approach used. CYCLE 2: Relatively short walls have been added to satisfy the open-front structure requirement, however further confirmation that all requirements are met is needed. Please address the following: a. Please clarify if the RISA lateral analysis assumes rigid diaphragms or semi-rigid diaphragms. If semi-rigid diaphragms are being used, please provide information on the inputs for walls and diaphragms and confirm the design follows the stiffness assumptions found in SDPWS 4.2.2 and 4.3.2.  b. Story drift limit per ASCE 7 Section 12.12 and SDPWS Section 4.2.5.2. Drift must be checked at the edges of the building where a torsional irregularity exists per ASCE 7 12.8.6. Provide calculations showing that story drift is not exceeded. Demonstrate that the analysis considers translation, rotation, and diaphragm shear/flexure displacements. c. Provide diaphragm calculations showing how the diaphragm was analyzed and designed based on the semi-rigid or rigid diaphragm assumption. For example, wood calculation page 99 shows only 1.11 kips of shear going to the "SWA.4A-R" shear wall that was added at the northwest corner. A majority of the story shear goes to the walls located along Grid D. How does the diaphragm deliver these forces to the Grid D walls? Show complete diaphragm calculations for determination of diaphragm forces, chord capacity, and diaphragm shear. How are diaphragm forces extracted from the RISA model in order to design the diaphragm?

Subject: Lateral Analysis
Comment: 18. WOOD LATERAL: Ref Struct Plans. AWC SDPWS-2015 Section 4.1.4 requires that all diaphragm boundary elements be capable of transferring design tension and compression forces. No straps or collectors are provided at re-entrant corners of the diaphragm, specifically at the exterior reentrant corners. Please comment on how diaphragm forces are transferred at these locations and add straps/collectors as required per the referenced code section. Include the following locations: (i) Grid A/3; (ii) Grid D/1; (iii) Grids C&E/7. CYCLE 2: Please address the following follow-up questions: a. The provided diaphragm calculation shown on wood calc page 107 illustrates a diaphragm support at the edges of the building. There are no shear walls at that location, why was a support assumed here? Furthermore the calculation appears to be based on a flexible diaphragm assumption, which is not valid for an open-front system. Revise diaphragm design to be consistent with the diaphragm assumption used for building design (rigid, semi-rigid, and/or flexible). b. The length of strap at the re-entrant corners may be inadequate considering the relatively large chord forces that are expected based on the distribution of shears going to the various shear walls (see comment #17c). For example, the strap at Grid D/1 extends 5 feet east. The diaphragm must be capable of transferring this force to the chord located to the north at the exterior of the building.  c. The diaphragm calculation on wood page 107 indicates a "solid block diaphragm". Where is the solid blocked diaphragm specified on the plans?

Subject: Wood Lateral
Comment: 21. HOLDOWNS: Ref S2.1. At many locations there are two holdown callouts adjacent to each other where double shear wall conditions exist. For example, there are two "T19" holdown callouts at the shear wall along Grid E, southern portion of the floorplate. The associated tension force per 12/S4.4 is 34 kips. Is the force acting on the concrete slab thus doubled (68 kips)? Please provide a sample calculation of how the tension forces shown on 12/S4.4 were determined. Identify where these forces are determined in the provided calculations. CYCLE 2: The response does not address how anchorage breakout per ACI Chapter 17 is achieved when two holdowns are in close proximity. Given that it's likely these anchor rods will be in tension simultaneously, how is this considered in the anchorage breakout design. Please provide breakout calculations that consider both anchors.

Subject: Wood Lateral
Comment: 22. HOLDOWNS: Ref Struct Calcs. Please address the following regarding the anchorage corner condition calculations starting on Concrete Calcs page 61/122: a. The calculations indicate that uncracked concrete is assumed, which is unlikely for a concrete transfer diaphragm in a high seismic region. Revise calculations to assume cracked concrete in accordance with ACI 318-14 Section 17.4.2.6 b. The calculations indicate that seismic loading requirements of ACI 318-14 Section 17.2.3.4.3 (a) is satisfied. However, the tensile force indicated does not appear to be adequate for assuming a ductile steel element. Revise the force to reflect the ACI seismic design requirement or provide further justification for the force used. CYLCE 2: Please address the following additional comments: c. It's unclear how the breakout design was accomplished for conditions where 12/S4.5 does not apply. There does not appear to be any anchorage reinforcement shown. For example, at T45 per 12/S4.4 "PAB8H" is specified with an allowable tension reaction of 31.7 kips. How are the requirements of ACI 318 Section 17.2.3.4.3 satisfied? Please provide calculations showing the concrete is capable of developing 1.2 times the nominal tensile strength of the anchor rod (option a) or show the connection is capable of resisting the earthquake load multiplied by omega (option d). d. At conditions where 12/S4.5 applies, the response is correct that this condition is not subject to ACI 318 Chapter 17 breakout requirements. The connection is subject to other ACI provisions that govern slab design when concentrated loads on a slab are present. Please provide calculations showing that the slab is capable of resisting the expected demand for two-way shear per ACI 318 Section 8.4.4. Include consideration of overstrength given that this is a Type 4 vertical irregularity per ASCE 7 Section 12.3.3.3.

Subject: Exterior Materials – High Quality
Comment: The Design Guidelines call for contextually appropriate high-quality materials that have sufficient thickness to prevent warping or deformation, do not require paint for a finish, are attractive when viewed up close, lend themselves to a high level of detailing, have integral color or texture and age well in Seattle ’s climate. The thin cementitious-fiber cladding materials are susceptible to poor installation and prone to degradation in appearance and performance over time in our climate. Staff and Design Review Board members have consistently expressed concern about the disparity between how these materials are represented in the Design Review documents (flat, plumb, square, true) and how they appear when installed. This view is borne out in multiple projects throughout the city and can result in significant maintenance and repair costs for building owners.  Staff therefore encourages project ownership and the design team to discuss this issue in depth, considering weathering characteristics and the associated trade-offs between life cost and initial cost when specifying exterior materials.  Staff strongly encourage applicants to explore options beyond the painted 5/16 ” fiber-cement products, as well as products with integral texture or inherent structural integrity (½ ”-plus/minus cementitious panels, phenolic resin, cementitious panels with integral texture and color, composite metal panel, etc.) to help mitigate this concern. (Design Guidelines DC4-A.1, CS3, DC4, DC4-A.2, DC4-1)Design Review (1)

Comment: [Revised and Repeated] SMC 22.170.110  (1) SDCI treats the rockery wall as erosion control features so it is only allowed when the slope shows adequate slope stability without rockery buttressing it. However, based on the geotechnical memo prepared by GeoResources dated 5/22/2024, the slope stability for the existing condition has FS=1.0. That means any excavation made below the existing rockery wall will cause the factor of safety to be less than 1.0. (2) The geotechnical memo prepared by GeoResources dated 5/22/2024 shows the proposed condition has FS=1.7 for static condition and 1.2 for seismic condition. However, the analysis done in these two conditions appear to not include the potential failure surfaces for the entire slope. (3) Rockery should not be given strength in the slope stability analysis. With above reasons, the proposed Rockery wall appears to be not feasible and the required factor of safety for the slope stability cannot be demonstrated. Please provide a different type of retaining wall system to address the proposed grade change. Please note when a different retaining wall system is proposed and if that requires a temporary cut at the toe of slope and existing rockery wall, please demonstrate the proposed excavation can be stable. Geotechnical review will continue in the next review cycle.

Subject: Performance monitoring notes
Comment: SMC 22.170.110 A. Please modify the shoring monitoring notes to reflect the following SDCI minimum monitoring requirements:   *Indicate on the plan the minimum monitoring point spacing along the top of the wall and minimum distance behind the wall that reflect the recommendations provided by the geotechnical engineer.   *Establish a baseline reading of monitoring points on the ground surface and settlement-sensitive structures behind the shoring wall alignment prior to dewatering, excavation, and installation of the shoring systems.   *A licensed surveyor (not the contractor) must do the surveying at least once a week.   *Survey frequency can be decreased after the shoring system has been installed and excavation is complete if the data indicates little or no additional movement. Surveying must continue until the permanent structure (including floor slabs as braces) is complete up to final and street grades. Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: When disturbing or removing trees or vegetation and/or adding, altering impervious surface is authorized a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan is required (SMC 25.09.065.B.5 and 25.09.070.C.1). The plan must be designed to compensate for any lost ecological function/s resulting from project impacts. Typically, the required mitigation area (in square feet) is equal to the combined areas of both temporary construction disturbance and permanent development (the total area of impact) but can vary based on the existing ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the ECA.    1. Based on existing ground coverage, provide a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan meeting the requirements of SMC 25.09.065.C. on sheet T2.0. You may use SDCI ’s standard ECA mitigation plan Seattle DPD Form - Standard Mitigation Plan or an alternative equivalent plan that includes the following:   ·A brief narrative or bulleted list summarizing how the mitigation plan compensates for lost ecological functions within the ECA. ·The location and size (in square feet) of the mitigation area(s). ·The location, size, species, quantities, and spacing of trees and vegetation to be newly planted. Plant quantities should be based on the size of the mitigation area and a multiplier sufficient to achieve a layered canopy. Shrub quantities can be determined by using multiplier 0.042 times the total area of impact that requires mitigation. Tree replacement can use a 0.01 multiplier or be 1:1.  ·Planting selections must be Pacific Northwest native species suited to specific site conditions/orientation. No cultivars or hybrids are allowed. ·New trees must be 4-6 feet in height or two-gallon size. Shrubs must be one-gallon size. ·Areas that have been cleared, graded, or compacted are to be amended with organic matter prior to planting with finely shredded mulch, minimum 4 ” depth between new plantings. Add The following standard note to your mitigation plan: The following monitoring and maintenance is required for a period of 5 years from date of plant installation. Self-monitoring is sufficient. No documentation is required to be submitted to SDCI unless requested. ·80 percent survival of new trees and vegetation planted at the end of five years; ·Annual inspections of the plants; ·Replacement of failed plants; ·Removal of exotic invasive species that have become established; and Photographic documentation of planting success retained for the five-year period

Comment: On the DWC Plan, please clearly show and label the perimeter foundation/footing drain discharge lines ( “FD” or “DRN ”) being routed directly to and passing through a catch basin prior to connecting to the new connection to the storm drain main in Madrona Drive. Footing drains cannot connect to the sanitary sewer or sanitary sewer main.   Per the Side Sewer Director's Rule 4-2011, Section VII.E.1 “Water collected by subsurface drains shall pass through a catch basin before discharge to a public system or watercourse …”  See also, Table C in Section VII.D.   Catch basins for footing drains must have a 2 ’ deep minimum sump and a sump volume of 2 cubic feet.   Footing drains, when applicable, must be routed separately from the downspouts and directly to an onsite catch basin prior to connecting to the approved point of subsurface discharge. Per the Side Sewer Director's Rule 4-2011, Section VII.C.5 “In no case shall downspouts be connected directly to a groundwater collection system or the tight line connection from a groundwater collection system. ” As mentioned above, please show and label a separate roof area storm drain collection system being routed to an onsite catch basin prior to connecting to the new connection to the storm drain main in Madrona Drive.   Because the footing drains and OSM BMPs overflow lines will all be routed to a storm main, overflow from the proposed OSM BMPs as well as the separate footing drains may join at a downstream catch basin prior to connecting to the storm main if/as needed. If multiple catch basins are needed, please show and label as such making sure to call out the overflow from the OSM BMPs and catch basin to the approved POD.

Comment: On the DWC Plan, where you call out the “new tree vine maple ”, please include that this tree is a required OSM BMP to mitigate Surface #3 per the stormwater code. With this, there are stairs on both the East and West sides of the proposed structure. Are both of these areas included in Surface #3?  If so, the stair at the West does not meet the requirements above as they are more than 20 ’ away from the proposed new tree.  Is there a retained tree near these stairs? If not, please separate this set of stairs and evaluate OSM BMP feasibility separately from the East stairs and if all BMPs end up being infeasible after working through the BMP Categories then you can select infeasible within the BMP Sizing tab for this set of stairs. OSM TREE REQUIREMENTS – Surface 3 (entry stairs) Trees:  Trees must be onsite and within 20-feet of the entire impervious surface area to be eligible for GSI/OSM credit. Existing Trees:  On the DWC Plan; show and label the size and species of the existing trees to remain for GSI/OSM mitigation. The trees must have a minimum 6-inch diameter (as measured 4.5-feet above ground) and meet the requirements of section 4.4.2.2 of the Seattle Stormwater Manual Volume 3. On the DWC Plan, please also call the tree(s) out where they stand as “Required for OSM Surface #xxx ” making sure to reference the individual Surface number they are to mitigate per the OSM Calculator. New Trees: On the DWC Plan; show and label the size, species, and number the trees to be planted for GSI/OSM mitigation including the hard surface identifier the tree corresponds with per the OSM Calculator. Trees eligible for On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) must be on the City of Seattle Master Tree List: https://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/Trees/PlantingAndCare/YardTrees/2011_street_tree_list. pdf Note: Trees in the "Small Category" are not eligible for mitigation. Deciduous must have a 1.5-inch minimum diameter as measured 6-inches above ground and evergreen trees must be a minimum of 4-feet tall and meet the requirements of section 5.2.4.2 and 5.2.5.2 of the 2016 Seattle Stormwater Manual Volume 3. On the DWC Plan, please also call the tree(s) out where they stand as “Required for OSM Surface #xxx ” making sure to reference the individual Surface number they are to mitigate per the OSM Calculator.  Tree Spacing:  In order to receive credit for GSI/OSM, the minimum tree spacing for newly planted trees shall accommodate mature tree spread as indicated in the City of Seattle Master Tree List https://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/Trees/PlantingAndCare/YardTrees/2011_street_tree_list. pdf  Please provide spacing that matches the tree spread indicated on the Tree List. Subject: 0 New Plan Review Process
Comment: FOR INFORMATION ONLY. NO RESPONSE REQUIRED On January 10, SDCI transitioned to providing plan reviews via plan mark-up instead of traditional letters. We appreciate your understanding as we rolled out the technology and staff learned new procedures. The primary change that we are asking of applicants is that they document responses to comments directly in the plan set provided to them by SDCI at the end of each review cycle instead of sending letters corresponding to each correction letter. When all responses are documented, we ask that applicants upload the response plan set (as document type Correction Response Plan Set or Correction Response Plan Set – Land Use) along with the new, clean plan set as (document type Plan Set or Plan Set – Land Use) for the next review cycle. We have a video to help you learn how to navigate the new process here:  https://youtu.be/KB8laufkd7M. As we transition to delivering marked up plan sets, you may receive both letters and marked up plan sets with our corrections documented. As a rule, please respond to any letter you receive with a letter and any marked-up plan set by embedding your responses in the marked-up plan set. We recognize that this transition requires changes to how you respond to our correction reports. We firmly believe that the changes we are instituting will lead to a reduction in the number of review cycles required to issue a permit. Remember, you will still: %ª Receive email notifications that a review has been completed. %ª Find review summary reports by discipline in the Seattle Services Portal as they are completed. %ª Submit updated plan sets after all reviews have been completed. What will be new is: %ª When all reviews are completed, you will receive a marked-up plan set which contains the comments from ALL the review disciplines. %ª Instead of preparing responses to each individual correction letter as you do today, you will be asked to reply to the comments directly in the marked-up plan set using either Bluebeam (requires a license) or Adobe Acrobat (free). If you work with subconsultants, you will need to coordinate with them to include their comments in your response plan set. Lastly, please help us perform reviews more efficiently! As we have worked on this transition, many of our reviewers indicated that they rely on bookmarks to navigate the (sometimes lengthy) plan sets that we receive from applicants. One thing that would allow us to review more quickly is to have applicants include a good set of bookmarks in every plan set that is submitted. Please follow the requirements for submitting pdf documents, outlined in Tip 106, General Standards for Plans and Drawings, to include a good set of bookmarks in every plan set you submit.Ordinance (2)

Subject: Drainage Review Required (OSM Required)
Comment: Drainage Review is required for this project per the 2021 Seattle Stormwater  Manual Volume 1, Chapter 8, since there is 750 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface and/or 5,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new and replaced hard surface associated with the project. Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas, driveways, walkways, and parking areas. Permeable pavement and pavers are considered a hard surface.      Please complete and submit the following documents: 1) Standard Construction Stormwater Control and Soil Amendment  (CSC/SOIL) Plan 2) Standard Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan 3) On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (full workbook) The following are the Approved Points of Discharge for the project: a) The "Approved Point of Stormwater Discharge" is "Curb weep". b) The "Drainage Basin" is "N/A for Single Family Projects". c) The "Approved Point of Wastewater Discharge" is "Sanitary Only" d) The "Approved Point of Subsurface Discharge" is "Onsite". The Seattle Stormwater Manual and all of the templates and documents mentioned above are available at http://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code. The CSC/SOIL Plan and DWC Plan must be combined with the submitted Plan Set PDF.

Subject: Code Modification Request
Comment: Sheet A7.07 and Code Modification Request - Sheet A7.07 - It appears that you are proposing to separate the stairway into two portions with 1-hr rated construction. If this is the design intent, the project will not require a code modification, since the stairway would then comply with SBC 1019.3. However, it is unclear to me whether the stairway separation is complete. Particularly at the open side of the stairs between basement and 1st level, I am having a hard time understanding if all of the stair's rated interior walls terminate at the rated ceiling. A 3-D diagram would be helpful to demonstrate the complete separation. Also, F4 floor assembly shows TJI members. This assembly does not describe the condition at stair landing and risers that use sawn lumber. Please provide 1-hr rated floor/ceiling assembly for the stair landings and risers.  - Code Modification Request -  Alternative to separating the stairs into two portions, a code modification request will allow vertical openings for exit access stairs connecting 5 stories without a shaft enclosure in R-3 occupancy. This is achieved by separating the stairway from the rest of the (basement) area on the lowest level.  If you would like to go with this method, sheet A7.07 shall be revised to show 1 hour fire barriers (highlighted in blue) and 1 hour doors (highlighted in green) at the basement level to separate the stair from the rest of the basement. Remove the 1-hr rated construction (your pink dash line) that was intended to separate the stairway into two portions.  Revise the Code Modification Request in the following area: 1. Description of Alternate/Modification:  - Clarify that the modification request is to allow vertical openings for exit access stairs connecting 5 stories (4 stories above grade + basement) without a shaft enclosure in R-3 occupancy. - Note that 1 hour fire barriers and 1 hour doors are proposed at the basement level to separate the stair from the rest of the basement.  - Additional details should be added to the package, including a basic plan showing the location of the stairway, wall+floor/ceiling+stair assemblies and door schedule.  2. Description of Code Requirement: - Add SBC 1023.2 Construction. "Enclosure for interior exit stairways... not less than 1 hour where connecting four stories or less." 3. Justification: The primary variance from the code requirements is that the exit access stairs connecting 5 stories (instead of 4) without a shaft enclosure in R-3 occupancies. Helpful information that supports your case for the code modification includes: - This exit access stairway is not used for basement egress.  - The stairway serves individual dwelling unit.  - The proposed separation at the basement level (1-hr rated wall and 1-hr rated door) is constructed with enclosure requirement for interior exit stairway connecting four stories to lessen hazard. 4. Include a "professional opinion" statement in the Justification section of the request. (See page 1 of the form) "When engaged for the project, the registered design professional ... safety, accessibility, and sanitation." I understand that this comment is quite complicated. Either route you choose to do (separating the stairs into two parts or Code-Mod with separating the stair bottom from the basement), please email me the revision prior to submitting for the next correction cycle (cici.sun@seattle.gov). We will review it internally and may need to set up a meeting to discuss. Thank you.Ordinance Structural (1)

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: Previous cycle correction (by Alan Lee):  Cycle 2: Per your response, SW 202, 102 & 106 uses FTAO methodology but do not show any collectors for shear transfer above and below openings. Please clarify. Current cycle correction:  AWC SDPWS-2015 section 4.3.5.2 Design for force transfer shall be based on a rational analysis. Typically, strength and rigidity of FTAO shear walls relies upon some horizontal axial connectivity of the horizontal panels to the vertical panels, right alongside the top and bottom of wall openings.  The written response letter and accompanying sketch acknowledges these forces, but states that your firm has conducted testing showing that certain shear walls do not need any horizontal collector element right along the top and bottom of openings.  In order for SDCI to accept testing in lieu of calculations, you will need to submit the test results as well as justification that the testing follows SBC protocols.  Therefore, either submit code-justified test findings from an approved agency, or else submit calculations demonstrating how the horizontal forces alongside the top and bottom of openings are transferred between the horizontal and vertical panels of the shear walls.

Comment: Revised Code of Washington (RCW) 64.55.005 requires that the developers of multi-unit residential buildings comply with one of the three options listed below. Indicate which option will be used and provide electronic copies of the required documents as specified. Option 1: a) Submit plans, details, and specifications for the construction of the building enclosure, per RCW 64.55.010(2). A final inspection will not be approved, nor a final certificate of occupancy issued prior to the receipt of the signed letter. Option 2: Submit a completed, signed, and recorded Condominium Sales Prohibition Covenant which prohibits the sale of individual dwelling units as condominiums for a minimum of five years. The completed and signed form must be recorded with the King County Recorder ’s office and submitted prior to permit issuance, per RCW 64.55.020(10). Option 3: Demonstrate RCW 64.55 does not apply by submitting an approved and recorded unit lot subdivision, prior to issuance of the construction permit.
