Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: Revegetation requirements apply within ECAs even if an exemption or other ECA relief is granted. The standards of SMC 25.09.070 apply when any of the following activities occur within ECAs: planting, disturbing, or removing trees and/or vegetation; adding, altering, or removing impervious surface; or other land disturbing activity. Please provide the following so we can determine the extent of tree and vegetation removal necessary and whether any impacts to ecological functions are adequately mitigated in the plan set. A. A1.0 or EXISTING landscape/site plan and table: Provide EXISTING ground coverage conditions. ECA code section SMC 25.09.065 requires that you avoid or minimize tree and vegetation removal within ECAs.  -  Provide total area of impact that requires mitigation: a. Total new hard surface area; b. Total temporary construction disturbance area  c. Use this calculation (a+b=c) for total area of impact that requires mitigation. - Provide a brief description of the EXISTING ground coverage within these areas. Examples of ground coverage include: lawn, ornamental landscaping, blackberry or other invasive species, trees, patio, pathway.  - Show locations of all existing trees to be removed and/or retained. Include a tree table with tree genus, species, common name, DBH (diameter at breast height), driplines, health, and if removed or retained. - Clearly delineate the "Steep Slopes (ECA1)"  and their buffers in the plan set.  - Include a brief summary of the existing ecological functions performed by the ECA on and adjacent to the site. The ecological functions include but may not be limited to: habitat for amphibian, avian, and terrestrial wildlife species; soil stabilization; and stormwater filtering, detention, and infiltration. B. PROPOSED landscape plan and table: Based on existing ground coverage, please show/delineate the PROPOSED mitigation in the form of replanting. Please update site plan and provide the information below: - The location, size, species, quantities and spacing of trees/shrubs to be newly planted per calculation on ECA standard mitigation plan. Tree replacement can be 1:1, shrub multiplier is 0.042 times total area that requires mitigation (see cor. A). https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Forms/TreeVegetationStandardMitigation Plan.pdf - New trees must be two gallon size (4'-6' in height) and shrubs one gallon.  - Planting selections shall be straight NATIVE species suited to specific site conditions/orientation, NO cultivars or hybrids are allowed. - Add a note that areas that have been cleared, graded, or compacted are to be amended with organic matter prior to planting. Use finely shredded mulch, minimum 4 ” depth between new plantings. - Clearly delineate the "Steep Slopes (ECA1)"  and their buffers in the plan set.  C. PROPOSED landscape plan in table: For existing trees proposed for removal SDCI requires that you demonstrate the use of required mitigation sequencing in the project development phase (SMC 25.09.065.B.1). These required steps are meant to find the least environmentally-damaging practicable alternative to achieve a project need to construct the updates you are proposing and trees you are proposing for removal.  Include items a. through f.in a table with responses to each. Additionally, show how you have considered of these items in order per SMC 25.09.065.B2. which states that the lower priority measures (b. through f.) shall only be applied if the higher priority measure (a.) is infeasible or inapplicable. Mitigation sequencing must be undertaken in the order of priority listed.    a. Avoiding the impact altogether by not taking a certain action or parts of an action; b. Minimizing impacts by limiting the degree or magnitude of the action and its implementation by using appropriate technology, best management practices, and/or by taking affirmative steps to avoid or reduce impacts; c. Rectifying the impact by repairing, rehabilitating, or restoring the affected environment; d. Reducing or eliminating the impact over time by preservation and maintenance operations; e. Compensating for the impact by replacing, enhancing, or providing substitute resources or environments; and f. Monitoring the impact and the compensation projects undertaken under subsection 25.09.065.B.1.e and taking appropriate corrective measures. D. PROPOSED landscape plan: Add the following standard notes to the landscape installation sheet/site plan: - The following monitoring and maintenance is required for a period of 5 years from date of plant installation. Self-monitoring is sufficient. No documentation is required to be submitted to SDCI unless requested. - 80 percent survival of new trees and vegetation planted at the end of five years; - Annual inspections of the plants; - Replacement of failed plants; - Removal of exotic invasive species that have become established;  - Photographic documentation of planting success retained for the five-year period; and - No permanent irrigation is allowed on erosion hazard areas or their buffers. E. A1.0, CSC, DWC Site plan: Provide a highly visible and durable protective barrier during construction to prevent access and to protect environmentally critical areas where applicable. Show on site plan around perimeter and include dimensions at fences so workers and inspectors can accurately site them in the field. Instead of using filter fence in ECA non-disturbance areas, use a less-invasive control measure, such as a compost sock (CS) at base of hi-vis fence. Detail (symbols) on CSC/Soil standard sheet.Revegetation (1)

Subject: General
Comment: [Sheet A1.1] The "NEW PLUS REPLACED HARD SURFACE AREA" calculation is incorrect.  The total new plus replaced hard surface area is 3,287 sf.   Please correct the calculations.  Note: per definition in the Seattle Stormwater Manual, Appendix A, “New hard surface ” means a surface that is: changed from a pervious surface to a hard surface (e.g., converting lawn to permeable pavement, resurfacing by upgrading from dirt to gravel, a bituminous surface treatment ( “chip seal ”), asphalt, concrete, or a hard surface structure); or upgraded from gravel to chip seal, asphalt, concrete, or a hard surface structure; or from a hard surface to a hard surface structure. Note that if asphalt or concrete has been overlaid by a chip seal, the existing condition should be considered as asphalt or concrete. Also, “Replaced hard surface ” or “replacement of hard surface ” means, for structures, the removal down to the foundation and replacement; and, for other hard surfaces, the removal down to existing subgrade or base course and replacement.Drainage (5)

Subject: For Projects over 1,500 S.F.
Comment: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2. Please submit the following with the next submittal: 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer.

Subject: Slope Stability Analysis for Infiltration in Steep Slope
Comment: This site is within the setback above an ECA Steep Slope or Landslide Prone Area where infiltration is limited. The ECA Steep Slope is located approximately 110 feet east of the site. Per Vol. 3, Section 3.2, Site Constraints, infiltration is limited within the slope or within a setback of 10 times the height of the slope to a maximum of 500 feet above the top of the slope.  Infiltration within this area may be feasible provided that a detailed slope stability analysis is completed by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer to demonstrate that infiltration facilities will not be harmful to the slope or adjacent properties. Please submit a slope stability analysis/infiltration impact analysis prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer and reference the analysis and distance from the ECA Steep Slope and/or Landslide Prone Area in the Drainage Report.

Subject: Seismic Site Class and Slope Stability Analysis
Comment: The uploaded geotechnical report assumed Site Class D to determine seismic coefficients. To categorize the site as Site Class D, please demonstrate one of the following criteria: a) Shear wave velocity for the top 100 ft is between 600 and 1,200 ft/s. b) SPT-N blow counts for the top 100 ft are between 15 and 50 per foot. c) Undrained shear strength for the top 100 ft is between 1,000 and 2,000 lb/ft². The subsurface explorations presented in the uploaded geotechnical report lack sufficient detail to determine the site class. As per Section 11.4.3 of ASCE 7-16, when soil properties are not known in sufficient detail to determine the site class, Site Class D is selected as the default site class, and the value of Fa shall not be less than 1.2 and site modified peak ground acceleration (PGAM) of 0.648 g should be used in slope stability analysis. Revise the seismic design parameters and update the slope stability analysis using site modified PGA.ECA GeoTech (4)

Subject: Slope Stability Analysis
Comment: Please provide an addendum to the geotechnical report that includes the revised slope stability analysis, input parameters (including infiltration rate and revised seismic coefficients), and analysis results, addressing the following comments: a) The reviewer believes the test pits in the original geotechnical report are insufficient to establish the soil profile. Please have a geotechnical engineer provide a detailed explanation of how the soil profile used for the slope stability analysis was depicted. b) A cohesion value of 100 psf was applied to the Advance Outwash. However, the reviewer believes that cohesion should not be considered for Advance Outwash. c) The entry and exit points used in the slope stability analysis are unclear. Please clearly identify and illustrate the entry and exit points, ensuring they are sufficient to capture the most critical slip surfaces. d) Clearly depict the groundwater table both before and after infiltration. e) Include the building load and any associated surcharge load in the analysis.

Subject: Stormwater Infiltration
Comment: The Onsite Stormwater Management Calculator states that infiltration is infeasible due to inadequate separation from groundwater/hard pan.  The supporting documentation says that is because the depth to hydraulically restrictive soils is 5 to 6 feet.  Per Appendix D of the Stormwater Manually, infiltration facilities are infeasible if there is less than 1 foot of vertical separation from hydraulically restrictive soils, so this infeasibility criteria is not applicable since there would be adequate depth to construct shallow infiltration facilities. The more significant issue, as mentioned in the "Infiltration Considerations" letter, is that the project site slopes down to the east, and that shallow perched groundwater could migrate to the adjacent building to the east which includes underground parking.  For this reason, the appropriate criteria for why infiltration is not feasible should be "Infeasibility criteria for "All infiltration BMPs" applies".  Per Appendix C of the Stormwater Manual, this includes "Infiltration is not recommended due to reasonable concerns about erosion, slope failure, or flooding", as documented in a signed and stamped written determination from a licensed professional and based on an evaluation of site-specific conditions. Please revise the Onsite Stormwater Management Calculator and and Drainage Report accordingly.

The risk assessment must document that the tree is considered a High  Risk hazard or that the tree has little or no likelihood of survival after construction. In making this  determination, the registered tree service provider must consider crown size, structure, disease, past  maintenance practice, potential damage to existing or future targets, risk mitigation options,  proposed demolition and construction methods, and the likelihood of survival after construction.  Tree service providers conducting commercial tree work on these trees must comply with the tree  service provider registry requirements of SMC Chapter 25.11Subsection 25.11.100. Subject: General
Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface. Comment: The Site Plan lists only 50sf of  the existing parking platform/deck as less than 36" above grade. However, the contours listed on the Site Plan shows that more than 50sf of the platform/deck may be more than 36" above grade. Per SMC.44.010.D.2.c "Decks or parts of a deck that are 36 inches or less above existing grade" are exempt from lot coverage.  Additionally, though the eaves appear to only extend 36 inches from the principal structure, the lot coverage calculations do not appear to include the gutters.   Per SMC 23.44.010.D.2.f. Please revise Lot Coverage diagram and calculations to correctly identify the structure(s) or portions of structure(s) included in the Lot Coverage.  When updating diagrams and calculations, please also include existing AND proposed lot coverage. Comment: Please add the following notes to the Temporary Erosion/Sedimentation Control Plan. These notes and requirements are in lieu of establishing a formalized seasonal grading restriction on the project and constitute the customary requirements that would be instituted for a seasonal grading extension:   A site visit from the Geotechnical Special Inspector shall occur during each day of active grading and in the event of significant rainfall which might compromise stabilization measures between November 1 and March 31. However, as a minimum standard, the Geotechnical Special Inspector is required to conduct a site visit if more than one-half inch of precipitation occurs on any given day. Any recommendations required to maintain stability of excavations and proper functioning of the sediment/erosion control system provided by the Geotechnical Special Inspector and SDCI personnel shall be implemented immediately. The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide copies of field reports to SDCI Site Development Services Section no later than 48 hours after each inspection. Comment: If you intend to use the existing side sewer/s, an Evaluation and Certification of the existing side sewers by a Professional Engineer is necessary because the existing side sewers were installed prior to 2004.  The necessary forms may be submitted prior to drainage approval of the building permit application, or a very clear, prominent boxed note added to the Civil Site Plan that the existing side sewer must be evaluated and certified prior to the connection to the side sewer.  Side Sewer Code 21.16.240 and the Requirements for Design and Construction of Side Sewers Director's Rule (DR 4-2011) detail the requirements for use of an existing side sewer.  In summary, a civil engineer must evaluate and certify the existing side sewer; if the side sewer is 50 years or older, the side sewer will need to be lined; if the existing side sewer is less than 50 years old, the line must either be lined, or the Evaluation and Certification process must include a pressure test. If, at this time, you do not intend to use an existing side sewer, please show and label a new connection to the sewer main.  This will also require further correction items and plan sheet notes with my next review.  The Side Sewer Evaluation and Certification Form is available with the following link: http://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/SDCI/Forms/SideSewerEvaluationCertification.pdf On the DWC Plan, please add a prominent boxed note that says, “Per Side Sewer Code 21.16.240, the existing side sewer must be Evaluated and Certified by a Professional Engineer and either Pressure Tested or Lined all the way to the public mainline in the street. ”

Subject: General
Comment: If you intend to use the existing side sewer/s, an Evaluation and Certification of the existing side sewers by a Professional Engineer is necessary because the existing side sewers were installed prior to 2004.  The necessary forms may be submitted prior to drainage approval of the building permit application, or a very clear, prominent boxed note added to the Civil Site Plan that the existing side sewer must be evaluated and certified prior to the connection to the side sewer.  Side Sewer Code 21.16.240 and the Requirements for Design and Construction of Side Sewers Director's Rule (DR 4-2011) detail the requirements for use of an existing side sewer.  In summary, a civil engineer must evaluate and certify the existing side sewer; if the side sewer is 50 years or older, the side sewer will need to be lined; if the existing side sewer is less than 50 years old, the line must either be lined, or the Evaluation and Certification process must include a pressure test. If, at this time, you do not intend to use an existing side sewer, please show and label a new connection to the sewer main.  This will also require further correction items and plan sheet notes with my next review.  The Side Sewer Evaluation and Certification Form is available with the following link: http://www.seattle.gov/documents/Departments/SDCI/Forms/SideSewerEvaluationCertification.pdf On the DWC Plan, please add a prominent boxed note that says, “Per Side Sewer Code 21.16.240, the existing side sewer must be Evaluated and Certified by a Professional Engineer and either Pressure Tested or Lined all the way to the public mainline in the street. ”

Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Even though you have oversized the drywells, please provide additional narrative as to the capacity of the drywells that are shown to include footing drains.  If the footing drains are shown being routed to the drywells in error, please correct as needed.   Please also more clearly show and label overflow from the drywells via catch basin connecting to the side sewer connection to the combined sewer main. Drywells shall have an overflow designed to convey any flow exceeding the capacity of the facility unless designed to fully infiltrate all flows for the full, required simulation period. If overflow is connected to the public drainage system, a catch basin shall be installed prior to the connection to the public drainage system to prevent root intrusion into public drainage main lines. To prevent damage to overlying pavement, drywells located beneath pavement shall be constructed with a trench pipe overflow connected to a catch basin with a grate cover. Design shall be such that, if the drywell infiltration capacity is exceeded, the trench pipe overflow would occur out of the catch basin to an approved point of discharge. The vertical elevation difference between the pavement surface and the trench pipe overflow invert shall be 1 foot minimum.

Comment: DWC Plan: "Permeable Pavement Surface (PPS)" is called out for the AADU Driveway.  The plans says this surface is to be "interlocking permeable plastic pavers and gravel".  Materials that are allowed to be counted as PPS are included in the "SPU Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials" document on the Stormwater Code webpage at http://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code (scroll down to "Reference Materials"). If it is not in the document, it will need to be demonstrated in the Drainage Report that it meets the following: Each paver shall be surrounded with an area of free-draining aggregate that is at least 10 percent of the area of the paver and the required storage reservoir below the paver shall be maintained. The free-draining aggregate surrounding each paver shall meet the requirements of the storage reservoir or the leveling course aggregates. The minimum required spacing between pavers is estimated by multiplying the required area by 2 and dividing by the perimeter of the paver per the following equation:  Spacing (between pavers) = 2 X Paver Area (square inches) X (10 percent) / Perimeter Length of Paver (inches).  Please clarify on the plan how the proposed PPS is meeting the minimum requirements above.5 (1)

Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Comment: Sheet A01: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2. Please submit the following with the next submittal … 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer*. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*. *Note: for Infiltration testing and plan preparation clarification for detached accessory dwelling units (DADUs) and additions with less than 1,500 sf of new plus replaced hard surface on lots with No Off-site Point of Discharge:   The applicant is allowed to perform the infiltration testing unless otherwise determined by the Director.   If the applicant chooses (in lieu of a licensed professional) to conduct the infiltration testing, the applicant shall conduct the Small PIT (rather than the Simple Infiltration Test).   The test shall be documented with the Pilot Infiltration Test Checklist and a minimum 0.25 in/hr measured soil infiltration rate must be demonstrated.   Drywells shall be sized, at a minimum, per Appendix E-10 - Drywell Sizing Tables of the  Seattle Stormwater Manual.   The applicant is allowed to prepare the drainage control plan unless otherwise determined by the Director.Drainage (2)

Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: AWC SDPWS 4.1.3 and ASCE 7-16 12.1 – Member strength and deformation compatibility.  Detail 2/S7.0 shows that shear wall boundary holdowns of upper levels are allowed to develop only into the shear wall of the level below (i.e. the upper wall ’s right side boundary element does not have aligned holdowns/studs continuous full-building height straight down into the foundation).  It is understood that the intent is that the shear wall at the level below distributes the upper level boundary holdown reaction outward to its own boundary members in shear.  As a horizontally-spanning member, this shear will also be accompanied by flexure (i.e. the lower wall acts as a deep beam).  The beam ’s moment and deflection diagrams would be those corresponding to the shear diagram shown on calculation page 473.  For this deep beam design approach, please justify that all elements are structurally adequate considering simultaneous forces and displacement compatibility, as follows: 1) To develop the intended resisting beam action, the lower shear wall will have to flex upward.  It does not appear, however, that there is a connection at the base of the lower wall or anywhere below it that is meant to “give” to allow this deflected beam shape to occur.  Clarify what is the mechanism that deforms/releases to allow the lower wall ’s deflected shape (and that such release does not result in a required load path having inadequate strength). 2) Initially until the lower wall deflects enough to carry the load horizontally through the plywood by beam action, it appears that the upper wall ’s boundary element in the lower wall will have the following load path:  the boundary element will pull up the lower wall ’s sheathing, such that the bottom of the sheathing will pull up its sheathing nailing which will pull the sill plate upwards in cross-grain bending, the sill plate will pull up on the rim board through its connectors, which will pull up the foundation sill plate through its connectors, and so on down all stories to the foundation (i.e. this is the initial de facto holdown load path).  Justify that all unreleased elements from the lower shear wall ’s sheathing on downward are adequate to resist the initial uplift force (in combination with other simultaneous forces) until the deep beam action engages. 3) For the flexure of the deep beam, it appears that the lower wall ’s top and bottom plates or rim joist potentially act as flanges (horizontal chords) of the beam (whether intended or not).  Within the calculations, clarify which elements are loaded by the flexure of the lower shearwall.  For elements that receive load as chords, demonstrate that all simultaneous loads within them and their connectors are accounted for (such as shear wall shear, horizontal shear flow for the beam action, external drag strut forces in the double top plate, etc.). 4) Ensure that any justifying calculations utilize code-required load combinations (such as .6D+.7E, if applicable).         ALL SCHEDULE

Current cycle correction:  SDCI is appreciative that you are providing a technical justification with calculations to support your position, as this is the best path toward resolving the deformation compatibility concern raised in our corrections.  Because of the uniqueness of this topic, you may email to the reviewer your follow-up response to this correction in-between review cycles, so as to help resolve it more quickly.  Following are some broader responses to your written responses: 1) The reason that SDCI does not view this detail the same as a flexible horizontal diaphragm is that a shearwall is restrained along its whole bottom edge.  If it were not, then we agree that it would be analogous to a horizontal flexible diaphragm (which typically does not have restraint to flexure along its far edge). 2) Your response mentioned that in a normally loaded shear wall, any incidental pulling up on the sill plate by the sheathing is ignored.  The difference to SDCI is that the testing that SDPWS shear wall tables are based upon accounted for the extent of that behavior that is caused by the shear wall resisting horizontal loading at the top of the shear wall.  Those tests, however, did not account for the simultaneous additional uplift from a concentrated vertical load introduced within the length of the shear wall. 3) Regarding the code sections mentioned in the original correction (AWC SDPWS 4.1.3 and ASCE 7-16 12.1), your response says that this portion of ASCE 7 does not support our concern.  SDCI disagrees as we do not see it stated therein that these code sections are limited to just the scenario you describe (gravity elements accommodating lateral displacement).  Within the subsections of 12.1 are general requirements that building elements shall be adequate to withstand forces and deformations they are subject to, which are the questions we are raising about this detail. 4) Based upon mechanics of materials, it is SDCI ’s position that the shear resistance of the wall that is being relied upon to carry the interior uplift force outward to the wall ends cannot be developed without the shear wall experiencing corresponding flexure (same as a beam that supports an interior point load).  In this detail, the beam (shear wall) is not being allowed to experience that necessary upward flexure because it is restrained all along its bottom edge.  Therefore, the upward load will not follow the more flexible shear path outward to the wall ends as you desire, but is instead being translated straight down through the sheathing into the sill plate.  We are concerned that this rigid load path downward will cause nails to tear out at the bottom of the sheathing, and sill plate cross grain bending, and uplift on the sill plate nails, and uplift on elements below. Assumedly, none of these elements were designed to carry this vertical load in addition to the forces they must resist for the shear wall ’s horizontal load. Due to length of this correction, see separate correction herein requesting specific further justification about the analysis you have provided. )

Comment: General Information / Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload a PDF of the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. These notes and requirements are in lieu of establishing a formalized seasonal grading restriction on the project and constitute the customary requirements that would be instituted for a seasonal grading extension:   A site visit from the Geotechnical Special Inspector shall occur during each day of active grading and in the event of significant rainfall which might compromise stabilization measures between November 1 and March 31. The determination of what constitutes significant rainfall is subject to the discretion of the Geotechnical Special Inspector. However, as a minimum standard, the Geotechnical Special Inspector is required to conduct a site visit if more than one-half inch of precipitation occurs on any given day. Any recommendations required to maintain stability of excavations and proper functioning of the sediment/erosion control system provided by the Geotechnical Special Inspector and SDCI personnel shall be implemented immediately.  The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide copies of field reports to SDCI Site Development Services Section no later than 48 hours after each inspection. Comment: Sheet DWC: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2. Please submit the following with the next submittal … 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer*. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*. *Note: for Infiltration testing and plan preparation clarification for detached accessory dwelling units (DADUs) and additions with less than 1,500 sf of new plus replaced hard surface on lots with No Off-site Point of Discharge:   The applicant is allowed to perform the infiltration testing unless otherwise determined by the Director.   If the applicant chooses (in lieu of a licensed professional) to conduct the infiltration testing, the applicant shall conduct the Small PIT (rather than the Simple Infiltration Test).   The test shall be documented with the Pilot Infiltration Test Checklist and a minimum 0.25 in/hr measured soil infiltration rate must be demonstrated.   Drywells shall be sized, at a minimum, per Appendix E-10 - Drywell Sizing Tables of the  Seattle Stormwater Manual.   The applicant is allowed to prepare the drainage control plan unless otherwise determined by the Director.Drainage (5)

Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Subject: Subgrade and bearing pressure
Comment: SMC 22.170.110 A.1.  Based on subsurface information and recommendations presented in the geotechnical report by Riley Group dated April 15, 2025  as well as desired bottom of footing elevations shown on 3/S3.1 and 4/S3.1, it appears that the proposed development will be supported on footing founded where the fill consisting of loose silt and silty sand was encountered in the exploration, B-1 and B-2, respectively. However, the geotechnical report recommended that the proposed structure be supported on conventional footings bearing on competent native soil or structural fill. Please revise the plan to include  (1) a foundation design and/or footing subgrade improvement that shows how the proposed development will be supported on the competent bearing soil and  (2) an excavation plan outlining the extent and slope of any excavation required to expose competent bearing soil. Alternatively, the plan could specify the depth needed for subgrade improvement to meet the geotechnical report's recommendations.

Comment: Based on the drip line of existing trees and the proposed project, it does not appear that any excavation and/or construction-related activity will occur within the tree protection areas of any on- or off-site trees. SDCI's standard tree and vegetation protection is not required. Please clearly note on the site plan a defined "development impact area." The development impact area is the area on the site affected by proposed site improvements, site access, storage/stockpiling of materials, or construction activities such as grading, filling, trenching, or other excavation necessary to install utilities or access. Include the following note on the site plan:  Tree Protection/Development Impact Area Requirements:  (1) Retention and protection of all trees 6 inches or greater is required.  (2) No tree removal or damage is authorized.  (3) Excavation and ground disturbance is prohibited outside of the development impact area. Comment: When disturbing or removing trees or vegetation and/or adding, altering impervious surface is authorized a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan is required (SMC 25.09.065.B.5 and 25.09.070.C.1). The plan must be designed to compensate for any lost ecological function/s resulting from project impacts. Typically, the required mitigation area (in square feet) is equal to the combined areas of both temporary construction disturbance and permanent development (the total area of impact) but can vary based on the existing ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the ECA. 1.Based on existing ground coverage, provide a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan meeting the requirements of SMC 25.09.065.C on new plan view sheet. You may use SDCI ’s standard ECA mitigation plan Seattle DPD Form - Standard Mitigation Plan or an alternative equivalent plan that includes the following: · A brief narrative or bulleted list summarizing how the mitigation plan compensates for lost ecological functions within the ECA. · The location and size (in square feet) of the mitigation area(s). · The location, size, species, quantities, and spacing of trees and vegetation to be newly planted. Plant quantities should be based on the size of the mitigation area and a multiplier sufficient to achieve a layered canopy. Tree replacement can use a 0.01 multiplier or be 1:1. · Planting selections must be Pacific Northwest native species suited to specific site conditions/orientation. No cultivars or hybrids are allowed. · New trees must be 4-6 feet in height or two-gallon size. Shrubs must be one-gallon size. Add the following standard note: The following monitoring and maintenance is required for a period · 80 percent survival of new trees and vegetation planted at the end of five years; · Annual inspections of the plants; · Replacement of failed plants; · Removal of exotic invasive species that have become established; and · Photographic documentation of planting success retained for the five-year period · Photographic documentation of planting success retained for the five-year period 3. In order to categorize as Site Class D, please demonstrate either of the followings: a)  Shear wave velocity for the top 100 ft is 600 to 1,200 ft/s b)  SPT-N blow counts for the top 100 ft is 15 to 50 per feet. c)  Undrained shear strength for the top 100 ft is 1,000 to 2,000lb/ft2. The subsurface explorations presented in uploaded geotechnical report does not sufficient detail to determine site class. As per Section 11.4.3 of ASCE 7-16, where the soil properties are not known in sufficient detail to determine the site class, Site Class D is selected as the default site class and the value of Fa shall not be less than 1.2. Please revise the seismic design parameters in a geotechnical report and update the structural design calculations accordingly.

Comment: If tree #5 is inside the steep slope buffer, you will need to document mitigation sequencing for the removal of the tree per the ECA code section SMC 25.09.065 [25.09.065.B] L01: ECA code section SMC 25.09.065 requires that you avoid or minimize tree and vegetation removal within steep slope ECAs. For existing trees proposed for removal SDCI requires that you demonstrate the use of required mitigation sequencing in the project development phase (SMC 25.09.065.B.1). These required steps are meant to find the least environmentally-damaging practicable alternative to achieve a project need to construct the updates you are proposing and trees you are proposing for removal. 1. Include items a. through f. in a table with responses to each. Additionally, show how you have considered these items in order per SMC 25.09.065.B2. which states that the lower priority measures (b. through f.) shall only be applied if the higher priority measure (a.) is infeasible or inapplicable. Mitigation sequencing must be undertaken in the order of priority listed.  a. Avoiding the impact altogether by not taking a certain action or parts of an action;  b. Minimizing impacts by limiting the degree or magnitude of the action and its implementation by using appropriate technology, best management practices, and/or by taking affirmative steps to avoid or reduce impacts;  c. Rectifying the impact by repairing, rehabilitating, or restoring the affected environment;  d. Reducing or eliminating the impact over time by preservation and maintenance operations;  e. Compensating for the impact by replacing, enhancing, or providing substitute resources or environments; and  f. Monitoring the impact and the compensation projects undertaken under subsection 25.09.065.B.1.e and taking appropriate corrective measures.

Subject: PE Evaluation & Certification Required
Comment: If you intend to reuse existing side sewer, an Evaluation and Certification of the existing side sewers by a Professional Engineer is necessary because the existing side sewer/s were installed prior to 2004.   SS Code 21.16.240 and the Requirements for Design and Construction of Side Sewers Director's Rule (DR 4-2011) detail the requirements for use of an existing side sewer. In summary, a civil engineer must evaluate and certify the existing side sewer; if the side sewer is 50 years or older, the side sewer will need to be lined; if the existing side sewer is less than 50 years old, the side sewer must either be lined or the Evaluation and Certification process must include a pressure test. Please add  a very clear, boxed note added to the Drainage and Wastewater Control Plan that  the existing side sewer must be Evaluated and Certified by a Professional Engineer and either rehabilitated (i.e. lined) or pressure tested all the way to the public mainline in the street.  The completed Evaluation and Certification form must be submitted to the inspector during construction.  The form is available with the following link: http://www.seattle.gov/dpd/permits/permittypes/sidesewer/default.htm

Indicate which option will be used and provide electronic copies of the required documents as specified. Option 1: a) Submit plans, details, and specifications for the construction of the building enclosure, per RCW 64.55.010(2). A final inspection will not be approved, nor a final certificate of occupancy issued prior to the receipt of the signed letter. Option 2: Submit a completed, signed, and recorded Condominium Sales Prohibition Covenant which prohibits the sale of individual dwelling units as condominiums for a minimum of five years. Subject: No POD requirements For Projects over 1,500 S.F.
Comment: See PAR #005329-23PA There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2.1. Please submit the following with the next submittal: 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer.

Please modify the shoring monitoring notes to reflect the following SDCI minimum monitoring requirements:  *Indicate on the plan the minimum monitoring point spacing along the top of the wall and minimum distance behind the wall that reflect the recommendations provided by the geotechnical engineer.  *Establish a baseline reading of monitoring points on the ground surface and settlement-sensitive structures behind the shoring wall alignment prior to dewatering, excavation, and installation of the shoring systems.  *A licensed surveyor (not the contractor) must do the surveying at least once a week.  *Survey frequency can be decreased after the shoring system has been installed and excavation is complete if the data indicates little or no additional movement. The survey frequency will be determined by the geotechnical engineer after review and approval by SDCI and SDOT.  *The geotechnical engineer shall review survey data and provide an evaluation of wall performance along with survey data to SDCI and SDOT on at least a weekly basis. At that amount of movement, the engineers and designers shall determine the cause of displacement and develop remedial measures sufficient to limit total wall movements to 1 inch. All earthwork and construction activities must be directed towards immediate implementation of remedial measures necessary to limit total wall movements to what has been defined as acceptable by the design team and SDOT (as indicated above).

Subject: No POD requirements For Projects over 1,500 S.F.

Indicate which option will be used and provide electronic copies of the required documents as specified. Option 1: a) Submit plans, details, and specifications for the construction of the building enclosure, per RCW 64.55.010(2). The building enclosure design documents must be signed and sealed by an architect or engineer licensed in the State of Washington, per RCW 64.55.10(3). b) Provide a statement on the plans or in a letter, signed and stamped as above, in substantially the following form: "The undersigned has provided building enclosure documents that in my professional judgment are appropriate to satisfy the requirements of RCW 64.55.005 through 64.55.090. ” c) Submit to the building inspector, a letter signed by a third-party qualified inspector certifying that the building enclosure has been inspected during construction and has been constructed in substantial compliance with the building enclosure design documents, per RCW 64.55.060. A final inspection will not be approved, nor a final certificate of occupancy issued prior to the receipt of the signed letter. Option 2: Submit a completed, signed, and recorded Condominium Sales Prohibition Covenant which prohibits the sale of individual dwelling units as condominiums for a minimum of five years. The completed and signed form must be recorded with the King County Recorder ’s office and submitted prior to permit issuance, per RCW 64.55.020(10). Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: This project was reviewed for consistency with SMC 25.09.070: Standards for Vegetation and Impervious Surface Management. The proposed project activities appear to be located within mapped steep slope environmentally critical areas (ECAs).  Revegetation requirements apply within steep slope ECAs even if an exemption or other ECA relief is granted. The standards of SMC 25.09.070 apply when any of the following activities occur within steep slope ECAs: planting, disturbing, or removing trees and/or vegetation; adding, altering, or removing impervious surface; or other land disturbing activity. It appears that the revegetation requirements for steep slope have not been met. Please provide the following so we can determine the extent of tree and vegetation removal necessary and whether any impacts to ecological functions are adequately mitigated in the plan set. ECA Revegetation (6)

Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: For the disturbance area in the steep slope ECA, provide a brief description/identification of the existing ground coverage within the area of temporary and permanent disturbance on CSC sheet, sheet A1.0, or new mitigation plan view sheet. Examples of ground coverage include: lawn, ornamental landscaping (vegetation species), blackberry or other invasive species, tree species, patio, pathway, driveway, stairway, etc. Calculate the area in square footage and show this on CSC sheet, sheet A1.0, or new mitigation plan view sheet. Provide a summary in a brief narrative or bulleted list of the existing ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the disturbed Steep slope ECA. The ecological functions include but may not be limited to: habitat for amphibian, avian, and terrestrial wildlife species; soil stabilization; and stormwater filtering, detention, and infiltration (SMC 25.09.065.C.2.a).

Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: .09.065.B]: ECA code section SMC 25.09.065 requires that you avoid or minimize tree and vegetation removal within steep slope ECAs. For existing trees proposed for removal (tree #386) SDCI requires that you demonstrate the use of required mitigation sequencing in the project development phase (SMC 25.09.065.B.1). These required steps are meant to find the least environmentally-damaging practicable alternative to achieve a project need to construct the updates you are proposing and trees you are proposing for removal. 1. Include items a. through f. in a table with responses to each on CSC sheet, sheet A1.0 or new mitigation plan view sheet. Additionally, show how you have considered these items in order per SMC 25.09.065.B2. which states that the lower priority measures (b. through f.) shall only be applied if the higher priority measure (a.) is infeasible or inapplicable. Mitigation sequencing must be undertaken in the order of priority listed.  a. Avoiding the impact altogether by not taking a certain action or parts of an action; b. Minimizing impacts by limiting the degree or magnitude of the action and its implementation by using appropriate technology, best management practices, and/or by taking affirmative steps to avoid or reduce impacts; c. Rectifying the impact by repairing, rehabilitating, or restoring the affected environment; d. Reducing or eliminating the impact over time by preservation and maintenance operations; e. Compensating for the impact by replacing, enhancing, or providing substitute resources or environments; and f. Monitoring the impact and the compensation projects undertaken under subsection 25.09.065.B.1.e and taking appropriate corrective measures.

Total temporary construction disturbance area including all construction-related activities including, but not limited to construction access, staging area, temporary excavation, and areas of tree/vegetation removal. c. Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: When disturbing or removing trees or vegetation and/or adding, altering impervious surface is authorized a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan is required (SMC 25.09.065.B.5 and 25.09.070.C.1). The plan must be designed to compensate for any lost ecological function/s resulting from project impacts. Typically, the required mitigation area (in square feet) is equal to the combined areas of both temporary construction disturbance and permanent development (the total area of impact) but can vary based on the existing ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the ECA.    1. Based on existing ground coverage within the area of impact in the steep slope ECA, provide a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan meeting the requirements of SMC 25.09.065.C. You may use SDCI ’s standard ECA mitigation plan Seattle DPD Form - Standard Mitigation Plan or an alternative equivalent plan that includes the following on CSC sheet, sheet A1.0, or new mitigation plan view sheet:    ·A brief narrative or bulleted list summarizing how the mitigation plan compensates for lost ecological functions within the ECA. ·The location and size (in square feet) of the mitigation area(s). ·The location, size, species, quantities, and spacing of trees/shrubs to be newly planted. Use the ECA standard mitigation plan as a guide only. Shrub quantities can be determined by using multiplier 0.042 times the total area of impact that requires mitigation. Tree replacement quantities can be 1:1 or alternatively use an adjusted tree multiplier of 0.01 as the ECA std. mit. plan multiplier results in an excessive number of trees. Goal is to provide a layered canopy. https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Forms/TreeVegetationStandardMitigation Plan.pdf ·Planting selections must be Pacific Northwest native species suited to specific site conditions/orientation. No cultivars or hybrids are allowed. ·New trees must be 4-6 feet in height or two-gallon size. Shrubs must be one-gallon size. ·Areas that have been cleared, graded, or compacted are to be amended with organic matter prior to planting with finely shredded mulch, minimum 4 ” depth between new plantings. Add the following standard note: The following monitoring and maintenance is required for a period of 5 years from date of plant installation. Self-monitoring is sufficient. For existing trees proposed for removal (tree #386) SDCI requires that you demonstrate the use of required mitigation sequencing in the project development phase (SMC 25.09.065.B.1). These required steps are meant to find the least environmentally-damaging practicable alternative to achieve a project need to construct the updates you are proposing and trees you are proposing for removal.   1. Include items a. through f. in a table with responses to each on CSC sheet, sheet A1.0 or new mitigation plan view sheet. Additionally, show how you have considered these items in order per SMC 25.09.065.B2. which states that the lower priority measures (b. through f.) shall only be applied if the higher priority measure (a.) is infeasible or inapplicable. Mitigation sequencing must be undertaken in the order of priority listed.   a. Avoiding the impact altogether by not taking a certain action or parts of an action;  b. Minimizing impacts by limiting the degree or magnitude of the action and its implementation by using appropriate technology, best management practices, and/or by taking affirmative steps to avoid or reduce impacts;  c. Rectifying the impact by repairing, rehabilitating, or restoring the affected environment;  d. Reducing or eliminating the impact over time by preservation and maintenance operations;  e. Compensating for the impact by replacing, enhancing, or providing substitute resources or environments; and f. Monitoring the impact and the compensation projects undertaken under subsection 25.09.065.B.1.e and taking appropriate corrective measures.

Comment: PARTIAL REPEAT: When disturbing or removing trees or vegetation and/or adding, altering impervious surface is authorized a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan is required (SMC 25.09.065.B.5 and 25.09.070.C.1). The plan must be designed to compensate for any lost ecological function/s resulting from project impacts. Typically, the required mitigation area (in square feet) is equal to the combined areas of both temporary construction disturbance and permanent development (the total area of impact) but can vary based on the existing ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the ECA.   1.Based on existing ground coverage within the area of impact in the steep slope ECA, provide a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan meeting the requirements of SMC 25.09.065.C. You may use SDCI ’s standard ECA mitigation plan Seattle DPD Form - Standard Mitigation Plan or an alternative equivalent plan that includes the following on CSC sheet, sheet A1.0, or new mitigation plan view sheet: Provide a brief narrative or bulleted list summarizing how the mitigation plan compensates for lost ecological functions within the ECA.  ·The location and size (in square feet) of the mitigation area(s). ·The location, size, species, quantities, and spacing of trees/shrubs to be newly planted. Use the ECA standard mitigation plan as a guide only. Shrub quantities can be determined by using multiplier 0.042 times the total area of impact that requires mitigation. Tree replacement quantities can be 1:1 or alternatively use an adjusted tree multiplier of 0.01 as the ECA std. mit. plan multiplier results in an excessive number of trees. Goal is to provide a layered canopy. https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Forms/TreeVegetationStandardMitigation Plan.pdf  Add notes: ·Planting selections must be Pacific Northwest native species suited to specific site conditions/orientation. No cultivars or hybrids are allowed.  ·New trees must be 4-6 feet in height or two-gallon size. Shrubs must be one-gallon size.  ·Areas that have been cleared, graded, or compacted are to be amended with organic matter prior to planting with finely shredded mulch, minimum 4 ” depth between new plantings.  ·Removal of exotic invasive species that have become established, and permanent irrigation is not allowed on ECA steep slopes

Comment: Drainage Review is required for this project per the 2021 Seattle Stormwater  Manual Volume 1, Chapter 8, since there is 750 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface and/or 5,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity. The Seattle Stormwater Manual and all of the templates and documents mentioned above are available at http://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code. The CSC/SOIL Plan and DWC Plan must be combined with the submitted Plan Set PDF.Drainage Review Required (OSM Required) (1)

Subject: Zoning - General and Special Corrections
Comment: Per 23.86.010.C.3, "On a lot with a rear property line, part of which is not essentially parallel to any part of the front lot line, the rear yard is measured from a line or lines drawn from side lot line(s) to side lot line(s), at least 10 feet in length, parallel to and at a maximum distance from the front lot line. If an alley abuts the rear of the property, 1/2 the width of the alley, between the side lot lines extended, is considered to be part of the lot for drawing this line. For those portions of the rear lot line that are essentially parallel to the front lot line, subsection 23.86.010.C.2 above shall apply. The lot depth is then measured perpendicularly from this 10 foot long line extended as needed to the point on the actual front lot line that is the furthest distance away. This establishes lot depth, which then may be used to determine the required rear yard depth." Since the rear lot line is not essentially parallel to the front lot line, please update rear yard accordingly.

Subject: DADUs & ADD/ALT less than 1500 S.F.
Comment: Sheet DWC: It appears from our mapping system that you would most likely be able to connect to an existing near side ditch/culvert in NE 125th Street. If this is not the case, and there is no ditch/culvert in NE 125TH street within frontage of this property, or this project is not able to discharge stormwater to this drainage ditch/culvert, then, the following is required: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2. Please submit the following with the next submittal … 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer*. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer*. *Note: for Infiltration testing and plan preparation clarification for detached accessory dwelling units (DADUs) and additions with less than 1,500 sf of new plus replaced hard surface on lots with No Off-site Point of Discharge:   The applicant is allowed to perform the infiltration testing unless otherwise determined by the Director.   If the applicant chooses (in lieu of a licensed professional) to conduct the infiltration testing, the applicant shall conduct the Small PIT (rather than the Simple Infiltration Test).   The test shall be documented with the Pilot Infiltration Test Checklist and a minimum 0.25 in/hr measured soil infiltration rate must be demonstrated.   Drywells shall be sized, at a minimum, per Appendix E-10 - Drywell Sizing Tables of the  Seattle Stormwater Manual.   The applicant is allowed to prepare the drainage control plan unless otherwise determined by the Director.Drainage (4)

Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload a PDF of the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. Comment: OSM TREE REQUIREMENTS & NOTES – Surface #5 (stairs) Trees:  Trees must be onsite and within 20-feet of the entire impervious surface area to be eligible for GSI/OSM credit. Existing Trees:  On the DWC Plan; show and label the size and species of the existing trees to remain for GSI/OSM mitigation. The trees must have a minimum 6-inch diameter (as measured 4.5-feet above ground) and meet the requirements of section 4.4.2.2 of the Seattle Stormwater Manual Volume 3. On the DWC Plan, please also call the tree(s) out where they stand as “Required for OSM Surface #xxx ” making sure to reference the individual Surface number they are to mitigate per the OSM Calculator. New Trees: On the DWC Plan; show and label the size, species, and number the trees to be planted for GSI/OSM mitigation including the hard surface identifier the tree corresponds with per the OSM Calculator. Trees eligible for On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) must be on the City of Seattle Master Tree List: http://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDOT/PublicSpaceManagement/2015-Street_Tree_List.p df Note: Trees in the "Small Category" are not eligible for mitigation. Deciduous must have a 1.5-inch minimum diameter as measured 6-inches above ground and evergreen trees must be a minimum of 4-feet tall and meet the requirements of section 5.2.4.2 and 5.2.5.2 of the 2016 Seattle Stormwater Manual Volume 3. On the DWC Plan, please also call the tree(s) out where they stand as “Required for OSM Surface #xxx ” making sure to reference the individual Surface number they are to mitigate per the OSM Calculator.  Tree Spacing:  In order to receive credit for GSI/OSM, the minimum tree spacing for newly planted trees shall accommodate mature tree spread as indicated in the City of Seattle Master Tree List http://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDOT/PublicSpaceManagement/2015-Street_Tree_List.p df  Please provide spacing that matches the tree spread indicated on the Tree List.

Comment: Tree Replacement Requirements (SMC 25.11.090):  Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 trees removed in association with development must be replaced by one or more new trees designed to result, upon maturity, in a canopy cover that is at least roughly proportional to the canopy cover prior to tree removal. Subject: 01 Administration
Comment: Informational for applicant on how to respond to city review comments: FOR INFORMATION ONLY.  In January 2022, SDCI transitioned to providing plan reviews via plan mark-up instead of traditional letters. We appreciate your understanding and patience as we rolled out the technology new to both applicants and SDCI staff.  The primary change that we are asking of applicants is that they document responses to comments directly in the plan set provided to them by SDCI at the end of each review cycle instead of sending letters corresponding to each correction letter. When all responses are documented, we ask that applicants upload the response plan set (as document type 'Correction Response Plan Set') along with the new, clean plan set as (document type 'Plan Set') for the next review cycle. This information is located at: https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/permits/how-to-respond-to-review-comments [If link is not active, cut and paste to URL] We have a video to help you learn how to navigate the new process here:  https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=KB8laufkd7M. [If link is not active, cut and paste to URL] As we transition to delivering marked up plan sets, you may receive both letters and marked up plan sets with our corrections documented. As a rule, please respond to any marked-up plan set by embedding your responses in the marked-up plan set. We recognize that this transition requires changes to how you respond to our correction reports. We firmly believe that the changes we have instituted will lead to a reduction in the number of review cycles required to issue a permit. Remember, you will still: %ª Receive email notifications that a review has been completed. %ª Find review summary reports by discipline in the Seattle Services Portal as they are completed. %ª Updated plan sets can only be submitted after all reviews have been completed. What will be new is: %ª When all reviews are completed, you will receive a marked-up plan set which contains the comments from ALL the review disciplines. %ª Instead of preparing responses to each individual correction letter as you do today, you will be asked to reply to the comments directly in the marked-up plan set using either Bluebeam (requires a license) or Adobe Acrobat Reader (free).. %ª If you work with sub-consultants, you will need to coordinate with them to include their comments in your response plan set. Lastly, please help us perform reviews more efficiently! As we have worked on this transition, many of our reviewers indicated that they rely on bookmarks to navigate the (sometimes lengthy) plan sets that we receive from applicants. One thing that would allow us to review more quickly is to have applicants include a good set of bookmarks in every plan set that is submitted. Please follow the requirements for submitting pdf documents, outlined in Tip 106, General Standards for Plans and Drawings, [https://www.seattle.gov/DPD/Publications/CAM/cam106.pdf] to include a good set of bookmarks in every plan set you submit. NOTE: VERIFY THAT BOOKMARKS ARE NOT BROKEN PRIOR TO RESUBMITTING PLAN SETS. Bookmark links can become broken when sheets are added or removed from the plan set.01 Administration (3)

Subject: General
Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload a PDF of the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable.
