Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload a PDF of the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Catch basins for footing drains must have a 2 ’ deep minimum sump and a sump volume of 2 cubic feet.  This must be called out on the DWC Plan. Comment: Lot Coverage.  Please confirm you've correctly counted all the chargeable areas in your lot coverage calculations and completed those calculations correctly.  For instance, it appears the projection over the basement stairs is ~3.5' x ~4.75' from the provided site plan which would equate to an additional 2.4 sq ft of chargeable lot coverage not included in your calculations, though from the site photos potentially that awning has been removed.  Please confirm. Also, I still have concerns that the deck and portions of the stairs adjacent are more than 36" above grade.  Given the number of risers shown on your site plan and the typical riser being ~7-8" in height this deck is likely elevated from grade between 42 and 48".  Even absent that, the covered portions of the deck, with the awning above should be included in your lot coverage calculations which would result in ~78-81 additional sq ft of lot coverage chargeable to this lot based on the height of that existing deck.  The site photos also exist that this deck and awning has potentially been removed as well, but I was unable to locate a permit application for the construction of the new deck. To that end, depending on the height of the attached deck your project may be over the lot coverage limit for this site.   Finally, it may be helpful if you provide additional information regarding the height of the deck and stairs, preferably in the form of a new permit application for the new deck more than 18" above grade with plans and that separate permit application could potentially qualify for issuance STFI.  See Tip 316 at https://www.seattle.gov/dpd/publications/cam/cam316.pdf for more info on STFI permits and https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/permits/do-you-need-a-permit for more info on when construction permits are required for work. Subject: 16 Lateral Design
Comment: Overturning at foundation S2.0 & Calcs L4 There is substantial overturning at the foundation at narrow and stacked shear walls. Clarify how the grade beam was designed for the overturning effects, shear, and moment. Verify that piles do not go into uplift. Notes have been made on the plans at a subset of other representative locations where overturning forces may govern. Response Per Structural Engineer:  Please see supplemental calculations on page P5 in the revised structural calculations verifying there is more dead load than uplift forces at the high load holdown locations. Cycle 2 Calcs P5. A) The wall has three supports, not two. Clarify why R1's idealized uplift load is not P1*5.5/8.5, like the downward load. B) It appears that the engineer has calculated the total dead load on the grid A wall, then compared it to the uplift load at R2. Please clarify the distributed load and the forces in the foundation along with the DL reaction at R1 and R2. C) Maximum shear is anticipated to be between the compression load and the tension load in the shearwall. Clarify how the shear in the foundaiton was designed for this force. D) Holdown loads are based on the distance between the compression and tension forces, which is narrower than the wall. This was changed in the 2021 SDPWS (4.3.6.1.2's B_eff). Clarify how this has been incorporated into the HD forces at the foundation.

Cycle 2 A) Rho only appears to have bee incorporated into the grid A earthquake loading. Per 12.3.4.2 and...chapter 12 in general...if rho = 1.3 in the north-south direction, it is to be applied throughout the design in the north-south direction, not just a single wall. Calcs L3 shows the shear to be 0.74+1.49+1.96 = 4.19k, which is less than the shear in the v1 of the calcs (1.5+2.7+1.3=5.5k). Verify that the shear on the walls matches the ELF calcs.

Subject: 401.5 Protection of Adjoining Propery
Comment: Per SRC R401.5 and Grading Code SMC 22.170.200 at window wells: It's not clear during cycle 1 review where the proposed window wells are located in the site plan.  However, assuming it is located at the west side of the lot, it's not clear if the height of the well as measured from the footing to top of wall is proposed taller than its horizontal setback from the west lot line.   Also, it is not clear how construction of the well will impact the neighbor to the west (or address property line protection issues).   Provide a section or excavation profile detailing the proposed excavation and construction of these window wells.  In the section profile, show that excavation for the new window wells do not exceed a 1-horizontal to 1-vertical (1H:1V) slope, and excavation does not encroach into the neighboring property.  If excavation doesn't meet any of the above, WITH your excavation profile, you MUST provide 1 or more of the following options as applicable (additional reviews may apply):   a) show that the vertical cut and height of the wall will not exceed 4-feet as measured from bottom of footing to top of wall; b) provide a letter signed by the impacted neighbor that provides written permission for temporary encroachment during construction.  Letter must specify the type and extent of encroachment, and confirm that the property must be restored to at least the original condition.  If this option is used because excavation encroaches into neighbor's property, note in site plan that letter is signed by neighbor, and upload letter separately; c) Or, provide proof that the properties are in common ownership;  d) Or, provide a RECORDED easement that is granted by the owner of the encroached-upon property, which authorizes the encroachment;  e) Or, provide engineered shoring plans meeting the recommendations of an accompanying geotechnical engineering report;  f) Or, provide a report by a geotechnical engineer providing justification for a temporary excavation slope steeper than 1H:1V. FINAL NOTE--the above assumes that the proposed site walls are completely constructed/built within the lot lines.  If any part of the wall is built across lot lines, additional reviews/permits may be required.

Subject: Performance monitoring notes
Comment: SMC 22.170.110 A. Please provide the shoring monitoring notes to reflect the following SDCI minimum monitoring requirements:   *Indicate on the plan the minimum monitoring point spacing along the top of the wall and minimum distance behind the wall that reflect the recommendations provided by the geotechnical engineer.   *Establish a baseline reading of monitoring points on the ground surface and settlement-sensitive structures behind the shoring wall alignment prior to dewatering, excavation, and installation of the shoring systems.   *A licensed surveyor (not the contractor) must do the surveying at least once a week.   *Survey frequency can be decreased after the shoring system has been installed and excavation is complete if the data indicates little or no additional movement. Surveying must continue until the permanent structure (including floor slabs as braces) is complete up to final and street grades. The survey frequency will be determined by the geotechnical engineer after review and approval by SDCI and SDOT.   *The geotechnical engineer shall review survey data and provide an evaluation of wall performance along with survey data to SDCI and SDOT on at least a weekly basis. Immediately and directly, notifyv SDCI and SDOT if any unusual or significantly increased movement occurs.   *Immediately and directly notify the geotechnical and structural engineers, wall designer, SDCI, and SDOT if 0.5 inches of movement occurs between two consecutive readings and when total movements reach 0.5 inch. At that amount of movement, the engineers and designers shall determine the cause of displacement and develop remedial measures sufficient to limit total wall movements to 1 inch. All earthwork and construction activities must be directed towards immediate implementation of remedial measures necessary to limit total wall movements to what has been defined as acceptable by the design team and SDOT (as indicated above).

Subject: General
Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload a PDF the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. Subject: General
Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project. Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference/when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  When drainage review is required, please ensure that you provide and are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  As part of the complete plan set, a Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates and/or standard plan notes. As a separate review document upload the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable. Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: Correction 1: General Information This project was reviewed for consistency with SMC 25.09.070: Standards for Vegetation and Impervious Surface Management. The proposed project activities appear to be located within mapped **steep slope environmentally critical area (ECAs) and their buffers. Revegetation requirements apply within ECAs even if an exemption or other ECA relief is granted. The standards of SMC 25.09.070 apply when any of the following activities occur within ECAs and their buffers: planting, disturbing, or removing trees and/or vegetation; adding, altering, or removing impervious surface; or other land disturbing activity. It appears that the revegetation requirements have not been *met. Please provide the following so we can determine the extent of tree and vegetation removal necessary and whether any impacts to ecological functions are adequately mitigated in the plan set. Correction 2: Existing Conditions Sheet 1. Provide an existing conditions plan. Clearly show the ** steep slope ECAs and their buffers (15 feet) on the existing conditions plan. 2. Provide a brief description/identification of the existing ground coverage within the area of temporary and permanent disturbance in the ECA. Examples of ground coverage include: lawn, ornamental landscaping (vegetation species), blackberry or other invasive species, tree species, patio, pathway, driveway, stairway, etc. Calculate the area in square footage and show this on the existing conditions plan. 3. Show locations of all existing trees located within and adjacent to the disturbance area consistently across all plan sheets. Include a tree table with genus, species, common name, DSH (diameter at standard height), dripline diameter and if trees/vegetation are proposed to remain or be removed. Please number trees consistently within table and across all plan sheets. 4. Provide a summary in a brief narrative or bulleted list of the existing ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the ** steep slope ECA. The ecological functions include but may not be limited to: habitat for amphibian, avian, and terrestrial wildlife species; soil stabilization; and stormwater filtering, detention, and infiltration (SMC 25.09.065.C.2.a). Revegetation (2)

Subject: Performance Monitoring Notes
Comment: SMC 22.170.110 A.  Given the depth of proposed excavation and the close proximity of temporary shoring to adjacent properties and structures, please include the shoring monitoring notes to reflect the following SDCI minimum monitoring requirements:  (1) Indicate on the plan the minimum monitoring point spacing along the top of the wall and minimum distance behind the wall per the geotechnical engineer's recommendations.  (2) Establish a baseline reading of monitoring points on the ground surface and settlement-sensitive structures behind the shoring wall alignment prior to dewatering, excavation, and installation of the shoring systems.   (3) A licensed surveyor (not the contractor) must do the surveying at least once a week.   (4) Survey frequency can be decreased after the shoring system has been installed and excavation is complete if the data indicates little or no additional movement. Surveying must continue until the permanent structure (including floor slabs as braces) is complete up to final and street grades. The survey frequency will be determined by the geotechnical engineer after review and approval by SDCI and SDOT.   (5) The geotechnical engineer shall review survey data and provide an evaluation of wall performance along with survey data to SDCI and SDOT on at least a weekly basis. Immediately and directly, notifyv SDCI and SDOT if any unusual or significantly increased movement occurs.   (6) Immediately and directly notify the geotechnical and structural engineers, wall designer, SDCI, and SDOT if 0.5 inches of movement occurs between two consecutive readings and when total movements reach 0.5 inch. At that amount of movement, the engineers and designers shall determine the cause of displacement and develop remedial measures sufficient to limit total wall movements to 1 inch. All earthwork and construction activities must be directed towards immediate implementation of remedial measures necessary to limit total wall movements to what has been defined as acceptable by the design team and SDOT (as indicated above).

This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Subject: 25.11.070.A.1.c
Comment: Tree #6 is a Tier 2 tree proposed for removal.  It would need to meet removal allowances under 25.11.070.A.1 if removal is to be approved.  It does not appear to meet 25.11.070.A.1.a or 25.11.070.A.1.b.   As described in TIP 242A, "A Tier 2 tree may be removed if necessary to construct proposed structures (such as a needed retaining wall or access for utilities) or to provide vehicular access to a site if necessary for proposed development. Tree removal under this scenario will not be authorized if there are viable alternatives to proposed development that would allow retention of the tree with adequate protection of the tree during construction according to SMC 25.11.060." Feel free to email me if you would like to discuss this correction.Tree (4)

Subject: Tree Replacement Requirements -- General
Comment: Tree Replacement Requirements (SMC 25.11.090):  Tree #7, a Tier 3 tree removed in association with development, must be replaced by one or more new trees designed to result, upon maturity, in a canopy cover that is at least roughly proportional to the canopy cover prior to tree removal. If Tree #6 is approved for removal, it also requires replacement. Replacement trees must also be native and/or culturally significant, and resilient to climate change (SMC 25.11.090.C.2). Please refer to Director ’s Rule 12-2023 for more information about tree replacement requirements. Please note that the GreenFactor Plant list referenced in this rule only lists bioretention trees, which are only appropriate in wet areas. Feel free to email me with species selection questions. Please note that street trees don't satisfy on-site tree replacement requirements.

Subject: PE Evaluation & Certification Required
Comment: If you intend to reuse existing side sewer, an Evaluation and Certification of the existing side sewers by a Professional Engineer is necessary because the existing side sewer/s were installed prior to 2004.   SS Code 21.16.240 and the Requirements for Design and Construction of Side Sewers Director's Rule (DR 4-2011) detail the requirements for use of an existing side sewer. In summary, a civil engineer must evaluate and certify the existing side sewer; if the side sewer is 50 years or older, the side sewer will need to be lined; if the existing side sewer is less than 50 years old, the side sewer must either be lined or the Evaluation and Certification process must include a pressure test. Please add  a very clear, boxed note added to the Drainage and Wastewater Control Plan that  the existing side sewer must be Evaluated and Certified by a Professional Engineer and either rehabilitated (i.e. lined) or pressure tested all the way to the public mainline in the street.  The completed Evaluation and Certification form must be submitted to the inspector during construction.  The form is available with the following link: http://www.seattle.gov/dpd/permits/permittypes/sidesewer/default.htm

Comment: Drainage Review is required for this project per the 2021 Seattle Stormwater  Manual Volume 1, Chapter 8, since there is 750 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface and/or 5,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity. Stormwater Code/Manual requirements are based on the amount of new and replaced hard surface associated with the project. Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas, driveways, walkways, and parking areas. Permeable pavement and pavers are considered a hard surface. Please complete and submit the following documents: 1) Standard Construction Stormwater Control and Soil Amendment  (CSC/SOIL) Plan 2) Standard Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan 3) On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (Note: Because the proposed amount of new and replaced hard surface is more than 750 square feet, but less than 1500 square feet, only the "Project Information" and "Site Information" section of the Project Summary tab in the OSM Calculator must be completed. Please enter the following information in the "Site Information" section of the Site and Drainage Control Summary Sheet: a) The "Approved Point of Stormwater Discharge" is "Curb Weep". b) The "Drainage Basin" is "N/A for Single Family Projects. c) The "Approved Point of Wastewater Discharge" is "Sanitary" d) The "Approved Point of Subsurface Discharge" is "On-site". Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: Correction A: General Information  This project was reviewed for consistency with SMC 25.09.070: Standards for Vegetation and Impervious Surface Management. The proposed project activities appear to be located within mapped **potential landslide prone environmentally critical areas (ECAs) and their buffers.       Revegetation requirements apply within ECA relief is granted. The standards of SMC 25.09.070 apply when any of the following activities occur within potential landslide prone ECAs and their buffers: planting, disturbing, or removing trees and/or vegetation; adding, altering, or removing impervious surface; or other land disturbing activity. It appears that the revegetation requirements have not been *met. Please provide the following so we can determine the extent of tree and vegetation removal necessary and whether any impacts to ecological functions are adequately mitigated in the plan set.    1. CSC, DWC: Add tree identifers on trees and note "See existing tree table on A0.1 or A0.3".  Correction B: Existing Conditions (A0.1, A0.3) 1. A0.1: Update tree schedule to remove Tier category number for trees and instead include "ECA" as trees in ECAs are not categorized by tier categories. This was done on A0.3. 2. A0.3: Provide a summary in a brief narrative or bulleted list of the  ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the ** potential landslide prone ECA. The ecological functions include but may not be limited to: habitat for amphibian, avian, and terrestrial wildlife species; soil stabilization; and stormwater filtering, detention, and infiltration (SMC 25.09.065.C.2.a).    Correction C: Project Impacts  A0.3, A0.4 and A0.5 show different calculations, update to follow the rule below. It appears the total should be closer to 5604 SF as noted on site plan. [25.09.065.C.2] Update to include on one sheet only to determine the total area of impact that requires mitigation using the calculation (a+b=c):  a. Total new hard surface area  b. Total temporary construction disturbance area including all construction-related activities including, but not limited to construction access, staging area, temporary excavation, and areas of tree/vegetation removal.   c. Total area of impact that requires mitigation in the form of replanting (use cor. Item 3 for multiplier of new shrubs required). Calculations should only include areas within property lines, as we cannot approve information on the adjacent property.    Correction D:  Proposed Mitigation  1. A0.5: On the mitigation plan, show the location, size, species, quantities, and spacing of trees/shrubs to be newly planted and those existing to be retained on site. Use the ECA standard mitigation plan as a guide only.   a. Shrub quantities can be determined by using multiplier 0.042 times the total area of impact that requires mitigation.   b. Tree replacement quantities can be 1:1 or alternatively use an adjusted tree multiplier of 0.01 as the ECA standard mitigation plan multiplier results in an excessive number of trees. The goal is to provide a layered canopy. Seattle DPD Form - Standard Mitigation Plan    References to help you choose native plants:   King County Native Plant Guide: Plant list - Native Plant Guide (kingcounty.gov)   WSU Native Plant Guide:WSU PNW Plants    2. Provide a summary in a brief narrative or bulleted list, an analysis of how the mitigation plan compensates for lost ecological functions within the ECA.    3. Add note stating:  a. Planting selections shall be Pacific Northwest native species suited to specific site conditions/orientation, no cultivars or hybrids are allowed.  b. New trees must be 4-6 feet in height and shrubs one-gallon size.  c. Areas that have been cleared, graded, or compacted are to be amended with organic matter prior to planting. Mulch, such as wood chips, should be added to a 3 ” thickness over the entire planting area without covering the stems of plants. Revegetation (1)

Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: When disturbing or removing trees or vegetation and/or adding, altering impervious surface is authorized a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan is required (SMC 25.09.065.B.5 and 25.09.070.C.1). The plan must be designed to compensate for any lost ecological function/s resulting from project impacts. Typically, the required mitigation area (in square feet) is equal to the combined areas of both temporary construction disturbance and permanent development (the total area of impact) but can vary based on the existing ecological functions performed by the trees and vegetation within the ECA.    1. Based on existing ground coverage within the area of impact, provide a mitigation (replanting/revegetation) plan meeting the requirements of SMC 25.09.065.C. You may use SDCIs standard ECA mitigation plan Seattle DPD Form - Standard Mitigation Plan or an alternative equivalent plan that includes the following:  ·A brief narrative or bulleted list summarizing how the mitigation plan compensates for lost ecological functions within the ECA. ·The location and size (in square feet) of the mitigation area(s). ·The location, size, species, quantities, and spacing of trees and vegetation to be newly planted. Plant quantities should be based on the size of the mitigation area and a multiplier sufficient to achieve a layered canopy. Tree replacement can use a 0.01 multiplier or be 1:1.  ·Planting selections must be Pacific Northwest native species suited to specific site conditions/orientation. No cultivars or hybrids are allowed. ·New trees must be 4-6 feet in height or two-gallon size. Shrubs must be one-gallon size. ·A note stating: Areas that have been cleared, graded, or compacted are to be amended with organic matter prior to planting with finely shredded mulch, minimum 4 ” depth between new plantings. ·A note stating: The following monitoring and maintenance is required for a period of 5 years from date of plant installation. Self-monitoring is sufficient. No documentation is required to be submitted to SDCI unless requested. ·80 percent survival of new trees and vegetation planted at the end of five years; ·Annual inspections of the plants; ·Replacement of failed plants; ·Removal of exotic invasive species that have become established; and ·Photographic documentation of planting success retained for the five-year period  128' 128'

Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Comment: Sheet DWC: There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Comment: On the DWC Plan – sheet C1.1, if applicable, please clearly show and label the perimeter foundation/footing drain discharge lines ( “FD” or “DRN ”) being routed directly to and passing through a catch basin prior to connecting to the onsite sanitary sewer connection to the combined sewer main. Catch basins for footing drains must have a 2 ’ deep minimum sump and a sump volume of 2 cubic feet.  This must be called out on the DWC Plan. Footing drains, when applicable, must be routed separately from the downspouts and directly to an onsite catch basin prior to connecting to the approved point of subsurface discharge. Per the Side Sewer Director's Rule 4-2011, Section VII.C.5 “In no case shall downspouts be connected directly to a groundwater collection system or the tight line connection from a groundwater collection system. ” Please clearly show and label a separate roof area storm drain collection system being routed to an onsite catch basin prior to connecting to the onsite sanitary sewer connection to the combined sewer main.  Because these lines will all be routed to a combined sewer main, overflow from the non-infiltrating bioretention planters as well as the separate footing drains may join at a downstream catch basin prior to connecting to the onsite sanitary sewer.  If footing drains are not proposed and/or required by another reviewer, please add a note on the DWC Plan that says, “Footing drains not proposed / required for this scope of work. ”  + WITH THIS, PLEASE ALSO UPDATE DWC PLAN NOTE #1D ACCORDINGLY.

For purposes of subsection SMC 23.44.041.C.2, the term “conversion ” means either keeping the accessory structure intact or removing and rebuilding the accessory structure, provided that any expansion or relocation of the accessory structure complies with the development standards for detached accessory dwelling units. Proof that the garage existed prior to December 31st, 2017 will need to be provided upon submitting corrections in order to convert the detached garage into a garage that is a part of a DADU. A previously approved plan set, survey, or aerial image dated prior to 12/31/18, will suffice as proof. If you do not wish to proceed with the breezeway connection, please remove all references to the breezeway as well as cloud the existing detached garage and provide a note on the site plan that says, “this permit does not establish the existing nonconforming garage for the record ”.

Comment: Revegetation requirements apply within ECAs even if an exemption or other ECA relief is granted. Please note that a portion of the rear yard is mapped with environmentally critical areas (ECAs) so all trees and vegetation regardless of size are protected, all regulated per the ECA code SMC 25.09. Existing landscape site plan/table: Provide EXISTING ground coverage conditions. ECA code section SMC 25.09.065 requires that you avoid or minimize tree and vegetation removal within ECAs.  - Provide a brief description of the EXISTING ground coverage within these areas. Examples of ground coverage include: lawn, ornamental landscaping, blackberry or other invasive species, trees, patio, pathway.  - Show locations of all existing trees on the property or trees whose branches overhang within the ECAs and their buffers. Include a tree table with tree genus, species, common name, DBH (diameter at breast height), driplines, health, and if they will be removed or retained. - Clearly delineate the "Steep Slopes (ECA1)" in the plan set. The SDCI External GIS Map is a helpful tool to locate designated ECAs. https://seattlecitygis.maps.arcgis.com/apps/webappviewer/index.html?id=f822b2c6498c4163b0cf 908e2241e9c2 - Include a brief summary of the existing ecological functions performed by the ECA on and adjacent to the site. The ecological functions include but may not be limited to: habitat for amphibian, avian, and terrestrial wildlife species; soil stabilization; and stormwater filtering, detention, and infiltration. 3. A0.6 Proposed landscape plan/table: Based on existing ground coverage, please show/delineate the PROPOSED mitigation in the form of replanting. Provide the information below: -It appears that area of patio removed totals approximately 470 SF. This will require mitigation in the form of replanting.  - The location, size, species, quantities and spacing of trees/shrubs to be newly planted per calculation on ECA standard mitigation plan. Tree replacement can be 1:1 if any were removed and shrub multiplier is 0.042 times total area 470 SF that requires 20 one-gallon native shrubs. https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Forms/TreeVegetationStandardMitigation Plan.pdf - Add notes to reflect number of new trees. Please demonstrate that the portion of each shearwall assumed as contributing to resisting end uplift does not exceed these length limitations.  Alternatively, if desiring to use dead loads from a greater extent of the shearwall length for resisting end uplift, submit calculations justifying that the shearwall construction has adequate strength and rigidity to transfer its dead loads from that far away to the wall end.

Comment: Per the Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.4.7.2, Permeable Pavement Facilities (PPF ’s) must meet the setback requirements for infiltration facilities presented in Section 4.3.  PPF’s must be 5 ’ from property lines (except for property lines fronting the public right-of-way), 5 ’ from buildings without basements. The infeasibility criteria provided for infiltrating facilities that setbacks cannot be met does not appear to be valid. There is ample room for permeable pavement facility (PPF) for a portion of the driveway. See markups on the Plan Summary Report. The area required for a PPF is 20% of the contributing roof area. For the SFR + AADU this would be 289 SF and 156 SF for the DADU. As the total contributing area would be more than 2,000 SF, either a Small Pilot Infiltration Test must be provided stamped by a licensed professional or the two contributing areas can be split into two facilities with a minimum of 10-ft setback between them. Again see the plan mark-up for a potential layout.  Another alternative is that there appears to be ample room in the front yard adjacent to the ROW for an infiltrating bioretention. Note that there is no required setback from the ROW.  Revise the DWC Plan and the OSM Summary Sheet to reflect any changes to the proposed BMPs. If infiltrating BMPs are not proposed and alternated justified infeasibility criteria must be provided.  If using PPF, show the following on the plans. The downspouts can connect to a catch basin and this catch basin can be the inlet and outlet to each of the PPF's. Then they can make a direct connection to the side sewer.  Clearly show the required setbacks, including 5-ft from the building foundations, 5-ft from the private property line and 10-ft between the facilities.  Clearly distinguish between the facility area and the surface area. The PPS will be the extents of the driveway with this required setbacks for the facilities.  Include the PPF standard detail on the DWC Plan replacing the bioretention detail.Eric Dripps (4)

Subject: Permeable Pavement Facilities Setbacks
Comment: Previous response fro Eric Dripps that has not been addressed. Per the Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.4.7.2, Permeable Pavement Facilities (PPF ’s) must meet the setback requirements for infiltration facilities presented in Section 4.3.  PPF’s must be 5 ’ from property lines (except for property lines fronting the public right-of-way), 5 ’ from buildings without basements. The infeasibility criteria provided for infiltrating facilities that setbacks cannot be met does not appear to be valid. There is ample room for permeable pavement facility (PPF) for a portion of the driveway. See markups on the Plan Summary Report. The area required for a PPF is 20% of the contributing roof area. For the SFR + AADU this would be 289 SF and 156 SF for the DADU. As the total contributing area would be more than 2,000 SF, either a Small Pilot Infiltration Test must be provided stamped by a licensed professional or the two contributing areas can be split into two facilities with a minimum of 10-ft setback between them. Again see the plan mark-up for a potential layout.  Another alternative is that there appears to be ample room in the front yard adjacent to the ROW for an infiltrating bioretention. Note that there is no required setback from the ROW.  Revise the DWC Plan and the OSM Summary Sheet to reflect any changes to the proposed BMPs. If infiltrating BMPs are not proposed and alternated justified infeasibility criteria must be provided.  If using PPF, show the following on the plans. The downspouts can connect to a catch basin and this catch basin can be the inlet and outlet to each of the PPF's. Then they can make a direct connection to the side sewer.  Clearly show the required setbacks, including 5-ft from the building foundations, 5-ft from the private property line and 10-ft between the facilities.  Clearly distinguish between the facility area and the surface area. The PPS will be the extents of the driveway with this required setbacks for the facilities.  Include the PPF standard detail on the DWC Plan replacing the bioretention detail.Permeable Pavement Facilities Setbacks (1)

Subject: Seismic Site Class justification
Comment: The uploaded geotechnical report assumed Site Class D to determine seismic coefficients. To classify the site as Site Class D, please demonstrate one of the following criteria: a) Shear wave velocity for the top 100 ft is between 600 and 1,200 ft/s. b) SPT-N blow counts for the top 100 ft are between 15 and 50 per foot. c) Undrained shear strength for the top 100 ft is between 1,000 and 2,000 lb/ft². The subsurface explorations presented in the uploaded geotechnical report lack sufficient detail to determine the site class. As per Section 11.4.3 of ASCE 7-16, when soil properties are not known in sufficient detail to determine the site class, Site Class D is selected as the default site class, and the value of Fa shall not be less than 1.2. However, the uploaded structural calculations use an Fa value of 1.0. Please revise the seismic design parameters in the geotechnical report and update the structural design calculations accordingly.

Comment: SMC 22.170.110 A. Please provide the shoring monitoring notes to reflect the following SDCI minimum monitoring requirements:  1) Indicate on the plan the minimum monitoring point spacing along the top of the wall and minimum distance behind the wall that reflect the recommendations provided by the geotechnical engineer.  2) Establish a baseline reading of monitoring points on the ground surface and settlement-sensitive structures behind the shoring wall alignment prior to dewatering, excavation, and installation of the shoring systems.   3) A licensed surveyor (not the contractor) must do the surveying at least once a week.  4) Survey frequency can be decreased after the shoring system has been installed and excavation is complete if the data indicates little or no additional movement. Surveying must continue until the permanent structure (including floor slabs as braces) is complete up to final and street grades. The survey frequency will be determined by the geotechnical engineer after review and approval by SDCI and SDOT.  5) The geotechnical engineer shall review survey data and provide an evaluation of wall performance along with survey data to SDCI and SDOT on at least a weekly basis. Immediately and directly, notify SDCI and SDOT if any unusual or significantly increased movement occurs.  6) Immediately and directly notify the geotechnical and structural engineers, wall designer, SDCI, and SDOT if 0.5 inches of movement occurs between two consecutive readings and when total movements reach 0.5 inch. At that amount of movement, the engineers and designers shall determine the cause of displacement and develop remedial measures sufficient to limit total wall movements to 1 inch. All earthwork and construction activities must be directed towards immediate implementation of remedial measures necessary to limit total wall movements to what has been defined as acceptable by the design team and SDOT (as indicated above).

Comment: Per the Preliminary Assessment Report 002877-24PA, there is no approved off-site point of discharge for drainage for this project.   Please submit plans and documents that comply with the following requirements from Section 4.3.2 of Volume 3 of the Seattle Stormwater Manual, "Requirements for Projects with No Off-Site Point of Discharge": a) The drainage control plan shall be prepared by a licensed civil engineer. b) Infiltration is feasible per Section 3.2 of Volume 3 of the Seattle Stormwater Manual, or infiltration is determined to be feasible as documented in a stamped and signed report from a licensed professional and approved by the Director.   c) In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration BMP shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow); and d) Infiltration BMPs shall be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). e) Identify the overland flowpath for flows that will exceed the capacity of the  infiltration BMP. Prevent the flows from causing erosion or flooding on site or on adjacent properties (refer to Section 4.3.3). If the flows will be directed towards an offsite building, structure or ECA Steep Slope or Landslide Prone area, then the infiltration BMPs shall be designed to fully infiltrate all flows for the full, required simulation period in the continuous runoff model (i.e., 100 percent infiltration). f) If the project site is within the setback from an ECA Steep Slope or Landslide Prone area where infiltration is limited a slope stability analysis is required per the Site Constraint section in Section 3.2. g) Overland flow path shall be vegetated and a minimum of 10 feet long between BMP and any property line (excluding right-of-way line).  h) Alternatively, if it is demonstrated that infiltration is not feasible as indicated above, all new and replaced hard surfaces shall be dispersed using Dispersion BMPs from Section 5.3.Drainage (1)

Subject: For Projects over 1,500 S.F.
Comment: If a connection to the public culvert is not feasible, the project must discharge onsite. See below for information on infiltration for this site. As the infiltration test provided does not meet minimum measured rate requirements for infiltration, either the site would need to provide an alternative infitlration test, possibly at an alternate location or increased depth to see if infiltration is feasible. Or the site would need to fully disperse. All roof surfaces would need to meet requirements for surface dispersion. Also the permeable pavement would need to meet a minimum 0.3 in/hr measured rate infiltration at a shallower depth than what was measured with the infiltration test. There is no available off-site point of discharge for drainage from this site. Where it has been determined by the Director that there is no off-site point of discharge (i.e. there is no public storm drainage system within the site frontage or that could be feasibly extended to the site) the project must infiltrate runoff from the area of development on-site. When infiltrating on-site, infiltration feasibility must first be demonstrated and the Drainage Control Plan (DWC Plan) must be prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer. In addition to meeting other minimum requirements for the project, the infiltration facility shall be designed to infiltrate the runoff volume from the area of development for the storm event with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence interval flow) and be sized so that overflows do not exceed 0.0001 cfs during the peak flow with a 4 percent annual probability (25-year recurrence flow). See Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 4.3.2.1. Please submit the following with the next submittal … 1.Small Pilot Infiltration Test (Small PIT) Checklist and supporting documents prepared by a licensed Geotechnical Engineer. 2.Drainage and Wastewater Control  Plan (DWC Plan) and Drainage Report prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer.  3.Drainage Report with a continuous runoff stormwater model prepared by a licensed Civil Engineer.

Subject: Grading season restriction notes
Comment: Please add the following notes to the Temporary Erosion/Sedimentation Control Plan. These notes and requirements are in lieu of establishing a formalized seasonal grading restriction on the project and constitute the customary requirements that would be instituted for a seasonal grading extension:   - A site visit from the Geotechnical Special Inspector shall occur during each day of active grading and in the event of significant rainfall which might compromise stabilization measures between November 1 and March 31. The determination of what constitutes significant rainfall is subject to the discretion of the Geotechnical Special Inspector. However, as a minimum standard, the Geotechnical Special Inspector is required to conduct a site visit if more than one-half inch of precipitation occurs on any given day.  - Any recommendations required to maintain stability of excavations and proper functioning of the sediment/erosion control system provided by the Geotechnical Special Inspector and SDCI personnel shall be implemented immediately.  - The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide copies of field reports to SDCI Site Development Services Section no later than 48 hours after each inspection. The field reports shall be uploaded to the special inspection record portal.  -The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide written notice that the site has been stabilized following completion of grading. Subject: Performance monitoring notes
Comment: SMC 22.170.110 A. Modify the shoring monitoring notes to include the following SDCI minimum monitoring requirements:   *Indicate on the plan the minimum monitoring point spacing along the top of the wall and minimum distance behind the wall that reflect the recommendations provided by the geotechnical engineer.   *Establish a baseline reading of monitoring points on the ground surface and settlement-sensitive structures behind the shoring wall alignment prior to dewatering, excavation, and installation of the shoring systems.   *A licensed surveyor (not the contractor) must do the surveying at least once a week.   *Survey frequency can be decreased after the shoring system has been installed and excavation is complete if the data indicates little or no additional movement. Surveying must continue until the permanent structure (including floor slabs as braces) is complete up to final and street grades. The survey frequency will be determined by the geotechnical engineer after review and approval by SDCI and SDOT.   *The geotechnical engineer shall review survey data and provide an evaluation of wall performance along with survey data to SDCI and SDOT on at least a weekly basis. Immediately and directly, notify SDCI and SDOT if any unusual or significantly increased movement occurs.   *Immediately and directly notify the geotechnical and structural engineers, wall designer, SDCI, and SDOT if 0.5 inches of movement occurs between two consecutive readings and when total movements reach 0.5 inch. At that amount of movement, the engineers and designers shall determine the cause of displacement and develop remedial measures sufficient to limit total wall movements to 1 inch. All earthwork and construction activities must be directed towards immediate implementation of remedial measures necessary to limit total wall movements to what has been defined as acceptable by the design team and SDCI (as indicated above). Subject: Grading season restriction notes
Comment: Please add the following notes to the Temporary Erosion/Sedimentation Control Plan. These notes and requirements are in lieu of establishing a formalized seasonal grading restriction on the project and constitute the customary requirements that would be instituted for a seasonal grading extension:  A site visit from the Geotechnical Special Inspector shall occur during each day of active grading and in the event of significant rainfall which might compromise stabilization measures between November 1 and March 31. The determination of what constitutes significant rainfall is subject to the discretion of the Geotechnical Special Inspector. However, as a minimum standard, the Geotechnical Special Inspector is required to conduct a site visit if more than one-half inch of precipitation occurs on any given day. Any recommendations required to maintain stability of excavations and proper functioning of the sediment/erosion control system provided by the Geotechnical Special Inspector and SDCI personnel shall be implemented immediately. The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide copies of field reports to SDCI Site Development Services Section no later than 48 hours after each inspection. The field reports may be emailed to sdcigeo@seattle.gov. The Geotechnical Special Inspector shall provide written notice that the site has been stabilized following completion of grading.

Comment: General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Single-Family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, deck/patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator. Comment: Please add dimensions to the plan demonstrating the minimum required setbacks below have been provided. Per the Seattle Stormwater Manual, Volume 3, Section 3.2,  infiltration facilities, must meet the following horizontal setback requirements:  5 ’ from property lines (except for property lines fronting the public right-of-way), 5 ’ from buildings without basements, and 10’ from buildings with basements.  Note: if runoff from 5,000 square feet or more of impervious surface area is infiltrated on the site, a building shall not intersect with a 1H:1V slope from the bottom edge of the infiltration BMP.

Subject: Tree Replacement Requirements (SMC 25.11.090)
Comment: Removal of on-site trees must meet tree replacement requirements. Tier 1, Tier 2, and Tier 3 trees removed in association with development must be replaced by one or more new trees designed to result, upon maturity, in a canopy cover that is at least roughly proportional to the canopy cover prior to tree removal. Replacement trees must also be native and/or culturally significant, and resilient to climate change (SMC 25.11.090.C.2). Please refer to Director ’s Rule 12-2023 for more information about tree replacement requirements. Please note that the GreenFactor Plant list referenced in this rule only lists bioretention trees, which are only appropriate in wet areas. Please choose a drought-tolerant species. Feel free to email me with species selection questions.

Subject: Tree Establishment (25.11.090)
Comment: Please add the following text in relation to the proposed replacement trees:   "For each relocated or required replacement tree, maintenance and monitoring is required for a five-year period. The period begins when the replacement tree is planted. Maintenance and monitoring shall include the following: 1.Sufficient maintenance actions to ensure survival of the replacement tree: a. When more than one replacement tree is required, 80 percent survival of new trees planted at the end of five years; b. When one replacement tree is required, 100 percent survival of the new tree planted at the end of five years; 2.Replacement and replanting of failed trees; and 3.Photographic documentation of planting success retained for the five-year period. Submission of documentation to the Seattle Department of Construction and Inspections is not required unless requested by the Department.

Subject: Permeable Pavement Surface feasibility
Comment: Repeat correction: The OSM Calculator indicates that Permeable Pavement Surfaces is not feasible because "30 A licensed professional (as defined in Appendix D, Section D-1) recommends permeable pavement not be used anywhere within the project site due to reasonable concerns of erosion, slope failure, or flooding (requires a signed and stamped written determination based on site-specific conditions from a licensed professional)." The geotechnical report does not seem to address permeable pavement surfaces directly, but only mentions general infiltration. The logs for  TP#2 and 3 suggest infiltration may be more feasible at the north edge of the site. This infeasibility criteria requires an evaluation of site-specific conditions and a written recommendation from a licensed professional (as defined in Appendix D, Section D-1). In January 2022, SDCI transitioned to providing plan reviews via plan mark-up instead of traditional letters. Minimizing impacts by limiting the degree or magnitude of the action and its implementation by using appropriate technology, best management practices, and/or by taking affirmative steps to avoid or reduce impacts; c. Rectifying the impact by repairing, rehabilitating, or restoring the affected environment; d. Reducing or eliminating the impact over time by preservation and maintenance operations; e. Subject: General
Comment: DRAINAGE REVIEW APPEARS TO BE REQUIRED General Information Note: Per SMC 22.807.020, drainage review is required when you are adding or replacing more than 750 square feet of hard surface along with other factors mentioned on the Stormwater Code website. Additionally, single-family projects with 7,000 square feet or more of land disturbing activity, 1,500 square feet or more of new plus replaced hard surface or, if on a lot or parcel created or reduced in size on or after January 1, 2016, must also implement On-site Stormwater Management (infiltration, dispersion, bio-retention, green roofs, permeable pavement, rainwater harvesting, etc.) to manage runoff from all hard surfaces on-site per SMC 22.805.030.B. and Director's Rule 21-2015.  This project is being reviewed under the 2021 Seattle Stormwater Code and Manual that went into effect July 1, 2021. Stormwater management requirements are based on the amount of new plus replaced hard surface (NPRHS) area associated with the project.  Examples of hard surfaces include roof areas with overhang/eaves, driveways, walkways, stairs, solid decking, patio and parking areas including pavement or gravel. Permeable pavement and pavers are also considered a hard surface.  When applicable, if decks and stairs are open slat and free draining to amended native soils below, please show and label as such on the Site Plan as well as the Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan when applicable. If not open slat and free draining, these areas must be included as a hard surface within the OSM Calculator.  For reference / when applicable: Allowable Permeable Pavement Wearing Course Materials For Stormwater Credit: https://www.seattle.gov/Documents/Departments/SDCI/Codes/StormwaterSPUAllowablePermeablePavem ent.pdf  Please ensure that you are always using the most current and up to date drainage and sanitary sewer related plan, forms, and documents from the Stormwater Code page and 2021 Seattle Stormwater Manual available at https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/codes/codes-we-enforce-(a-z)/stormwater-code including:  Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan and Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan templates (when applicable and if not already included in the complete plan set) and/or standard plan notes.  Please note that even if drainage review is not required, a completed Standard Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan is required to be included in the complete plan set when there is any ground disturbance.  As a separate review document upload a PDF of the completed Onsite Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator (version 01-04-2023 or newer) including the completed Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator on the DWC Plan. Updated standard plan BMP details on the DWC Plan or DWC Details Plan sheet when applicable.  As part of the complete plan set, please submit the following: A completed Standard Drainage and Wastewater Control (DWC) Plan including the Site and Drainage Control Summary from On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator.  Insert in line with the Construction Stormwater Control and Post Construction Soil Management (CSC/Soil) Plan in the plan set. As a separate upload, please also submit a PDF of the entire completed On-site Stormwater Management (OSM) List Approach Calculator for review and retention. Without it, I cannot fully review or approve OSM BMP ’s.  Note: If On-site Stormwater Management is not required for the scope of the work, you do not have to submit a PDF of the OSM Calculator for review however, the Site and Drainage Control Summary from the OSM Calculator must still be completed and present on the DWC Plan as mentioned above leaving only the Infiltration and On-Site Stormwater Management sections at the bottom blank.Drainage (15)

Subject: 301 Design Criteria
Comment: Per SRC 301.1 & SBC 1609.1.1 Kzt value in lateral wind design:  In sheet S0, under code summary, and unless missed elswhere, the Kzt value for lateral wind design appears missing (including in the structural calculations).  The topographic factor, Kzt, as described in ASCE 7-16, Section 26.8.2 shall be considered in wind design of the building.  The Kzt factor for this location is approximately 2.00, obtained online at: https://www.seattle.gov/sdci/resources/wind-load-factors.  You may either:  a) Revise the design using this mapped value, OR b) Provide calculations to justify the use of another factor.  The calculations shall include a plan view of the topographic area, clearly showing all significant elevation points, and a profile for each critical direction.  Note that the critical direction may not necessarily be from the steepest slope, and that the downwind effects may govern the calculation of the factor K2.  See the SEAW commentary on wind code provisions, ATC 60 vol. 1, section 6.4.Ordinance Structural (3)

Comment: If applicable, please clearly show and label the perimeter foundation/footing drain (FD or DRN) discharge lines being routed directly to and passing through a catch basin that meets the following requirements prior to connecting to the approved point of discharge as noted within this letter.  Per the Side Sewer Director's Rule 4-2011, Section VII.E.1 “Water collected by subsurface drains shall pass through a catch basin before discharge to a public system or watercourse …”  See also, Table C in Section VII.D.   Catch basins for footing drains must have a 2 ’ deep minimum sump and a sump volume of 2 cubic feet. This must be clearly called out in the DWC Plan. Footing drains, when applicable, must be routed separately from the downspouts and directly to an onsite catch basin prior to connecting to the onsite sanitary sewer connection. Because these lines will all be routed to a combined sewer main, these collection lines may join at a downstream catch prior to connecting to the onsite sanitary sewer. Subject: Subgrade and Bearing Pressure
Comment: (Revised and Repeated Item) SMC 22.170.110.A.1. Based on test pit logs presented in the Geotechnical report, dated June 26, 2024, competent bearing soils were generally encountered at about Elevation 231 feet, with the exception of northwest portion of the site. Test pits TP-2 and TP-3 in the southern portions of the site encountered up to 8 feet of LOOSE fill soils. Caving was observed in both of these two test pits, indicating a LOOSE condition.  However, based on plan sheets A1.00 and A1.02, the block walls are shown to bear on structural fill placed over up to 12 feet of LOOSE fill soils (based on information from test pits TP-2 and TP-3). In addition, some elevation views show additional weight (significant thickness of structural fill and structures) will be added to the slope, increasing the hazard of future earth movement given the underlying loose soil conditions. The ECA code requirement is that the proposed development meets complete stabilization. Upload an addendum to the geotechnical report that includes methods that demonstrate complete stabilization for the final grading condition, particularly on the southern project area. Include supporting calculations and evaluations to demonstrate complete stabilization in the addendum, and update the plan set accordingly.  SDCI reviewer will continue review in the next review cycle. ECA GeoTech (6)

Comment: 10. GRADE BEAMS CYCLE #1: SBC 1810.3.12 and ACI 318-14 18.13.3.2 - Revise grade beams to show closed ties. Structural calculations dated 10/12/2024 appear to indicate that shear reinforcing is required along some portions of several beams per ACI 318-14 Section 9.6.3.1. Provide reinforcing or clarify why shear reinforcing is not provided.  If reinforced concrete slab-on-grade is used as seismic tie, provide calculations that demonstrate compliance with SBC 1810.3.13 and clearly indicate that the slab-on-ground is a structural diaphragm and part of the seismic-force-resisting system per ACI 318-14 section 18.13.3.4. Revise details of connection of slab-on-grade to grade beams and pile caps as needed to show positive connection. CYCLE #2: It appears that calculations have been revised to suggest that stirrups are not required, but several issues persist.      A. Site Class:  Section 5.1 of geotechnical report states: "According to Chapter 20 of ASCE 7, the site soil should be classified as Site Class F because of its liquefaction potential during a strong seismic event." Site Class D is only used for determining site coefficients based on the assumption that the vibration period for the buildings is less than 0.5 second. Revise S1.0 to indicate Site Class F.      B. Foundation ties:  Per ASCE 7-16 section 12.13.8.2: Individual pile caps, drilled piers, or caissons shall be interconnected by ties. In addition, individual spread footings founded on soil de ﬁned in Chapter 20 as Site Class E or F shall be interconnected by ties." The grade beams do not have closed ties as required by ACI 318-14 18.13.3.2, and slab-on-grade is not designed as a diaphragm per ACI 318-14 18.13.3.4, therefore, ties appear to be missing. Revise plan set to provide ties per ACI 318-14 section 18.13.3.2 or 18.13.3.4.      C. Vertical loads due to shear wall overturning: Calculations do not include loads at ends of shear walls due to seismic and wind loading. Revise calculations to include upward and downward reactions at ends of shear walls due to lateral loads.      D. Shear reinforcing: Plan set appears inconsistent with calculations. For example, calculations for SFR/AADU grade beam T-7 assume 60" overall depth, and plan S3.1 refers to GB1/S2.3 which indicates 2'-0" minimum depth. If this grade beam is constructed as only 2'-0" deep per minimum depth dimension specified in detail GB1/S2.3, it will require stirrups.  Similarly, calculations for DADU grade beam T-3 assume 12" width, while sheet S3.3 refers to GB1/S2.3 which indicates an 8" wide grade beam. Revise plan to indicate minimum beam depths that are consistent with calculations and that result in beam designs that do not require shear reinforcing, or revise plans to show shear reinforcing in grade beams that require it. Comment: 12. ELEMENTS SUPPORTING DISCONTINUOUS WALLS OR FRAMES CYCLE #1: ASCE 7-16 Section 12.3.3.3 - Structural elements supporting discontinuous shear walls shall be designed to resist the seismic load effects including overstrength factor. Overstrength factor shall be applied to seismic load effects for all elements and connections in the load path, from location of discontinuity to the foundation  (i.e. beams, connections, columns, etc.)  Verify all locations where elements support discontinuous walls or frames. Revise plans and calculations to demonstrate that all elements and their connections in the load path to the foundation are adequate to resist all loads and consider all directions of loading.  For example: Calculation for beam (1-1) (5-1/4" x 11-7/8" PSL supporting Level 2 shear wall E33 on grid 1 of SFR) appears to be provided on page 181-182 of 337 of structural calculations, however, calculations do not appear to consider any seismic loading or overstrength. Similarly, calculations for beam (1-5) which appears to cantilever to support the aforementioned beam (1-1) appear to be shown on page 190-191 of 337 of structural calculations, but do not show a cantilever condition and seismic load appears to be significantly too low, and uplift capacity of CCQ connection appears to be insufficient for holdown load amplified by overstrength factor. There are several other locations where loads are discontinuous and appear to require strengthening to provide adequate load path to foundations. Revise calculations and plans and demonstrate compliance at all discontinuous shear walls. CYCLE #2: Thank you for the written response, and clarifying the page numbers, however, the issue noted in Cycle #1 persists. In the example noted in Cycle #1, calculations for beam (1-1) (5-1/4" x 11-7/8" PSL supporting Level 2 shear wall E33 on grid 1 of SFR) appears to be provided on pages 122-126 of 337 of Cycle #1 structural calculations, and it appears that overstrength was not considered. Page 16 of 337 indicates a seismic uplift of 4,639 lbs which would increase to 11,597 lbs including overstrength (=4639*2.5), but calculations on pages 124-126 indicate a seismic load of only 5,200 lbs (5.2 kips). It is unclear how 5.2 kips was calculated. As noted in Cycle #1, revise calculations and plans and demonstrate that all framing and connections are adequate at all discontinuous shear walls. For example, it appears that for beam (1-1), the uplift demands due to seismic overturning will exceed the capacity of the HUCQ hanger provided. Calculations shall clearly indicate the implementation of Overstrength Factor, which (as noted in Cycle #1) shall be applied for for all elements and connections in the load path, from location of discontinuity to the foundation (i.e. beams, connections, columns, etc.) Note that Figure C12.3-5 in ASCE 7-16 was incomplete and was revised in ASCE 7-22 to clarify code intent. 5 14 x 11 78 PSL (1-1)

Subject: ECA Revegetation
Comment: Mitigation Sequencing [25.09.065.B]: ECA code section SMC 25.09.065 requires that you avoid or minimize tree and vegetation removal within steep slope ECAs. For existing trees proposed for removal SDCI requires that you demonstrate the use of required mitigation sequencing in the project development phase (SMC 25.09.065.B.1). These required steps are meant to find the least environmentally-damaging practicable alternative to achieve a project need to construct the updates you are proposing and trees you are proposing for removal. 1. Include items a. through f. in a table with responses to each. Additionally, show how you have considered these items in order per SMC 25.09.065.B2. which states that the lower priority measures (b. through f.) shall only be applied if the higher priority measure  (a.) is infeasible or inapplicable. Mitigation sequencing must be undertaken in the order of priority listed. a. Avoiding the impact altogether by not taking a certain action or parts of an action;  b. Minimizing impacts by limiting the degree or magnitude of the action and its implementation by using appropriate technology, best management practices, and/or by taking affirmative steps to avoid or reduce impacts;  c. Rectifying the impact by repairing, rehabilitating, or restoring the affected environment;  d. Reducing or eliminating the impact over time by preservation and maintenance operations;  e. Compensating for the impact by replacing, enhancing, or providing substitute resources or environments; and  f. Monitoring the impact and the compensation projects undertaken under subsection 25.09.065.B.1.e and taking appropriate corrective measures.

Subject: Special Inspector nomination
Comment: SMC 22.170.130. Nominate a geotechnical engineering firm on the SDCI Geotechnical Special Inspections Schedule form. The form  is named as " Special Inspection Notification" and can be found on the project portal. This form must be signed by the owner or owner's representative; the form cannot be signed by the contractor nor the geotechnical engineer.      The Inspection Agency must be the same engineer/firm that prepared the geotechnical report. If the owner nominates a different engineer/firm to act as the Geotechnical Special Inspector, the new engineer must review the original geotechnical report and submit a letter indicating a review was performed, along with a statement of agreement with the evaluation and provisions contained in the report. If the new engineer does not agree with aspects of the report, rebuttal evaluations and recommendations must be included in the review letter. The plans must be revised accordingly and submitted to SDCI for review. Please do not fill in special inspection items on the enclosed form.    Requests for changes of Special Inspection Agency that occur during plan review should be submitted with corrected plans. If the request occurs after permit issuance, send the materials to the geotechnical reviewer. SS
